Headline: Osaka’s G20 summit likely to impede logistics operations from June 27-30
Details:
Japan will host its first ever Group of Twenty (G20) summit at Osaka’s International Exhibition Center on June 28-29, 2019. The G20 summit is held annually for governments of 20 member nations to discuss a wide range of issues affecting the world’s economy. In light of the high profile event, Japanese authorities have released a statement detailing large-scale traffic and sea restrictions near Osaka Port, Kansai International Airport (KIX), as well as within Osaka city during the summit period. As KIX is the country’s third largest airport and a key logistics hub for engineering and automotive companies from southern and central regions of Japan, heightened security checks and restrictions may significantly affect cargo handling and delivery for industries that rely heavily on this route. 

Organizers of the G20 summit reportedly aim to reduce traffic by 50 percent for four days, during and leading up to the event. To this end, local authorities have set up traffic restrictions in and around Osaka especially for roads connecting to KIX. The airport is built on an artificial island in Osaka Bay; thus the bridge that connects KIX to Rinku town on the main island will be the most impacted route, particularly on June 27 and June 30 during the arrival and departure of head of states. 

From June 27-30, 10 major sections of Hanshin Expressway including No.1 Loop Route and the Gulf Line totaling about 160 kilometers that connects to KIX, hotels, and the summit venue will be closed to traffic from morning until late evening to facilitate movement of delegates and participants of the summit. As a result, traffic will likely be diverted to other expressways such as Meishin Expressway. In Osaka, traffic restrictions will be in effect at 9 locations: Osaka Station, Nakanoshima, Tenma, Osaka Castle, Honcho, Uehoncho, Namba, Tennoji, and Nanko. 

In order to access international cargo and fuel supply areas, authorities have set up a fixed route bus that goes from Kansai Airport Station to these areas. However, the bus may not operate normally due to traffic restrictions and logistics providers have been advised to allow for extra travel time. 

According to official statements by the local authorities, heightened security checks can be expected at three main entry points in Kansai region: Kansai International Airport, Osaka International Airport (also known as Itami Airport), and Kobe Airport. Due to their proximity to the event venue, Kansai and Osaka Airports will be used widely by the participants and both airports have released statements pertaining to cargo inspections. 

While no airlines have publicly announced additional flights during the aforementioned period, both airports have pre-warned about possible flight delays on June 27 and June 30 due to the arrival and departure of aircrafts carrying heads of states and government officials. Both airports also have prohibited flying drones above and around the facilities; KIX in particular has restricted flying drones within 1,000 meters of the airport. 

According to the statement released by authorities, all vessels entering the sea near Osaka Port and KIX from June 24–30 are requested to provide prior notification to Japan’s maritime security department by noon at least the day before the planned navigation date. Failure to do so would result in longer berthing times. Shipping companies can submit earlier notifications to the nearest maritime security department starting from June 3–19. In addition, vessels are also requested to refrain from entering designated restricted areas, referred to as ""voluntary navigation restraint sea area"", around the airport island and the ""exclusive use sea area"" between the two parts of the island.

Traffic restrictions in and out of KIX for 4-days are likely to be the main challenge for Everstream Analytics customers with airfreight as collection service for KIX from major domestic shipping companies and delivery service centered in Osaka are likely to be disrupted, particularly on June 27 and 30. In addition to road restrictions, security spot checks on vehicles and cargo inspections may take longer than usual prior to and during the summit.

It is possible that local freight forwarders may pick up imported air cargo arriving during the G20 summit period from July 1 onwards. Thus, customers are advised to liaise with local contacts to avoid delays for critical cargo, such as perishable or pharmaceutical goods, that may require special handling. Alternatively, customers can also consider rerouting shipments to Tokyo’s Narita Airport to avoid delays. This option was used by manufacturers when KIX was shut down for 3-days due to the destruction caused by Typhoon Jebi in 2018.

Headline: COVID-19 Causing Backlog of Cargo at Karachi Port; 180 Trucks Stranded at Libya-Tunisia Border
Details:
On Thursday, Pakistani media sources reported that as of April 15, some 1,900 shipping containers had accumulated at Karachi Port due to a decision by the government to halt trade with neighboring Afghanistan amid the COVID-19 pandemic. However, officials indicated that they expected the backlog to ease in the near future, as while the Pakistani government extended a nationwide shutdown and restrictions on public gatherings for another two weeks on April 14, some so-called “low-risk” industries have been allowed to reopen, including construction, agriculture, e-commerce, paper, and packaging, among others, with export orders to resume soon as well. Meanwhile, Libyan media outlets reported that 180 cargo trucks have been stranded at the country’s border with Tunisia for several weeks due to COVID-19-related travel restrictions. The trucks are reportedly loaded with foodstuffs bound for Libya but have been unable to enter the country or return to Tunisia due to the countries’ respective coronavirus containment efforts, which include the closure of their shared border.



Assessment: The developments highlight how efforts to contain COVID-19 have negatively affected supply chains in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA). Indeed, commercial shipping operations largely continue throughout region, as, despite many countries having curbed cross-border travel, air, sea, and overland cargo shipments have generally been exempt from such directives. Still, coronavirus-induced restrictions, notably mandatory quarantines, nightly curfews, and enhanced screening procedures, have reduced the capacities of some service providers, delayed cargo handovers and inspections, and extended lead-times, among other issues, leading to incurring storage and demurrage at ports and delays at borders for customs. With some MENA nations having begun to relax such measures, associated disruptions may soon start to dissipate. That said, residual backlogs and service delivery delays should be anticipated.

Headline: Mutant Virus Strain May Result in Produce Shortages, Supply Chain Disruptions, Rising Prices in UK
Details:
On Saturday, December 19, British Prime Minister Boris Johnson announced a new set of restrictive measures due to the emergence of a novel mutant strain of the SARS-CoV-2 virus that causes COVID-19. Preliminary analyses indicate that the strain, which has been dubbed VUI-202012/01, is approximately 70 percent more effectively transmitted from person to person than the existing variant of SARS-CoV-2. The World Health Organization has stated that there is currently no indication that VUI-202012/01 results in more severe COVID-19 than the existing variant of the virus, nor does it possess higher morbidity. As of this writing, there has been no indication that current COVID-19 vaccines are less effective against this variant of the virus. New restrictions imposed across England include shifting areas such as London into Tier 4, wherein residents are to stay at home with the exception of essential activities, and non-essential international travel is banned. Media reports have emerged indicating that additional police units are being deployed to transport hubs such as train stations across the affected areas to enforce compliance with restrictive measures. Furthermore, a number of countries in Europe, including Germany, the Netherlands, France, and Switzerland, as well as elsewhere, have imposed a precautionary ban on travel into their respective territories from the UK for the foreseeable future. While there were no indications of associated bans on travel from mainland Europe into other countries in the region at the time of this writing, it is worth noting that VUI-202012/01 has reportedly also been detected in Denmark, Belgium, and the Netherlands. 



Media reports have emerged indicating that associated restrictions and travel bans are resulting in disruptions to cargo transport, and British ports, which have already been under pressure due to COVID-19 restrictions and a recent uptick in worldwide container traffic, are under increasing strain. Royal Mail has purportedly suspended deliveries of packages and letters from the UK to mainland Europe, and postal services from other countries in the region, such as Germany, to the UK and the Republic of Ireland have likewise been suspended for the foreseeable future. The European Union held a meeting to discuss the bloc’s response to the emergence of VUI-202012/01 on December 21; however, there were no indications as to any conclusions drawn from the meeting known at the time of this writing. 



Assessment: While the novel mutant strain of SARS-CoV-2 is reportedly not associated with higher morbidity, a surge in daily new deaths in the UK is likely in the foreseeable future off the back of rising daily case incidence resultant from higher transmissibility of VUI-202012/01. As the vaccination campaign progresses in the country, community immunization efforts may mitigate the negative impacts of the recent outbreak of this strain. It is worth noting, however, that media reports have emerged suggesting that this strain initially emerged in the UK in September but remained at low levels nationwide until mid-November, when its transmission may have been propagated by an unspecified “super-spreader” event. As such, the possibility that further restrictive measures on movement and/or gatherings may be imposed across England in the coming days and weeks in an effort to curb viral spread cannot be ruled out. 



Tier 4 restrictions and travel bans imposed on the UK by other countries are likely to incur supply chain disruptions to businesses from a variety of sectors, such as manufacturing, due to delays in imports and exports or cancellations of deliveries. Such disruptions are likely to result in financial losses to impacted organizations and, as daily case incidence in the UK is currently on an incremental trajectory, the possibility that these restrictions and associated disruptions may persist for the coming weeks cannot be ruled out. Disruptions to cargo transport may result in shortages of produce, including food, and associated rising prices within the UK for the foreseeable future. It is worth noting, however, that government officials have indicated that only some 19 percent of daily freight traffic is foreseen to be affected by travel bans and other restrictions. It is advised to continue monitoring developments associated with the emergence of VUI-202012/01 in the UK and elsewhere, related restrictions on transit and cargo transport, and heightened police presence across Tier 4 areas. Moreover, it is recommended to be vigilant to the potential for disruptions to supply chains through the UK and possible future shortages of produce in the country.

Headline: CORRECTION: Conditions gradually improve at after court orders Transnet Port Terminals strike halt
Details:
A previous version of this incident mistakenly classified it as an industrial fire and has now been corrected. 

Reports indicate that a company-wide go-slow strike began at the end of June after the state-owned port operator Transnet Port Terminals failed to disburse an anticipated bonus payment to employees. The strike has resulted in vessel berth waiting times of 4 to 5 days at the Port of Durban, where 60% of South African imports and exports are processed. Unspecified equipment failures are further complicating matters at the port. However, the most severe impacts are at Ngqura Container Terminal near Port Elizabeth, where total waiting times for berths have increased to 7 days or more. At both locations, shipping companies indicated that they are incurring losses of USD 25,000 each day due to the delays, prompting some vessels to bypass ports. Disruptions have also been reported at Port Elizabeth Container Terminal and in Cape Town. Some carriers, such as MSC, Maersk, and ONE have announced the employment of extra loaders in an attempt to minimize delays during port calls in South Africa. 

At Ngqura Container Terminal, container loading has slowed from 25 containers per hour to between 5 and 8 containers per hour. This has had a significant impact on local agricultural cargo, particularly citrus exporters who are in high season between the months of February and August. Citrus industry representatives additionally noted that the go-slow strike has exacerbated pre-existing challenges with low crane capacity, limited cold storage capacity, and limited container availability. 

Volkswagen, one of the container terminal’s largest customers, utilizes the terminal as a critical transit point for parts supplied to their assembly plant in Uitenhage. The plant is missing its production target of 680 units per day by approximately 400 units. Losses are expected to intensify if critical parts for the just-in-time manufacturing process do not arrive soon. A vessel with 150 containers including some critical automotive parts is reportedly in the Nelson Mandela Bay area but has not yet managed to berth at the terminal. Reports indicate that trucks have been forced to wait for up to 18 hours for inbound and outbound shipments, with members of local meat, textile, and electronics industries also reporting ground transportation disruptions.  

Expert testimony to media suggests that the cause of the strike was a critical failure in judgment by Transnet managers. Historically, Transnet has announced incentive bonus payments on the morning that financial statements are released to the public. Such an announcement was anticipated at the end of June and it is understood that employees were under the impression that bonus payments would be processed at that time in a regular fashion. However, the financial statement release has been delayed by an ongoing audit that is not likely to be concluded until mid- August, and Transnet is not able to disburse the funds until the audit is completed. 

As the end of June neared, with funds for bonus payment disbursal inaccessible until the audit is completed, Transnet managers issued a new stipulation that bonus payments will be paid to employees on the condition that employees have met on-time-performance targets, a proposal that was reportedly rejected by some workers. While labor unions representing Transnet employees chose not to resort to industrial action, non-unionized workers expressed frustration at the handling of the matter and organized their own strike. As evidence of their frustration, this action was executed without sanctioning from South African courts, which protects employees from being fired for strike participation.  At least 11 employees have been suspended for their participation. 

On July 14, Transnet announced that it has obtained an interdiction from the Labor Court of Port Elizabeth that orders striking employees to halt their action. Reports on July 15 indicated that performance at Transnet Port Terminals was already improving. Delays are likely to persist as backlogs are cleared.

CORRECTION: Conditions gradually improve at after court orders Transnet Port Terminals strike halt A previous version of this incident mistakenly classified it as an industrial fire and has now been corrected. 

Reports indicate that a company-wide go-slow strike began at the end of June after the state-owned port operator Transnet Port Terminals failed to disburse an anticipated bonus payment to employees. The strike has resulted in vessel berth waiting times of 4 to 5 days at the Port of Durban, where 60% of South African imports and exports are processed. Unspecified equipment failures are further complicating matters at the port. However, the most severe impacts are at Ngqura Container Terminal near Port Elizabeth, where total waiting times for berths have increased to 7 days or more. At both locations, shipping companies indicated that they are incurring losses of USD 25,000 each day due to the delays, prompting some vessels to bypass ports. Disruptions have also been reported at Port Elizabeth Container Terminal and in Cape Town. Some carriers, such as MSC, Maersk, and ONE have announced the employment of extra loaders in an attempt to minimize delays during port calls in South Africa. 

At Ngqura Container Terminal, container loading has slowed from 25 containers per hour to between 5 and 8 containers per hour. This has had a significant impact on local agricultural cargo, particularly citrus exporters who are in high season between the months of February and August. Citrus industry representatives additionally noted that the go-slow strike has exacerbated pre-existing challenges with low crane capacity, limited cold storage capacity, and limited container availability. 

Volkswagen, one of the container terminal’s largest customers, utilizes the terminal as a critical transit point for parts supplied to their assembly plant in Uitenhage. The plant is missing its production target of 680 units per day by approximately 400 units. Losses are expected to intensify if critical parts for the just-in-time manufacturing process do not arrive soon. A vessel with 150 containers including some critical automotive parts is reportedly in the Nelson Mandela Bay area but has not yet managed to berth at the terminal. Reports indicate that trucks have been forced to wait for up to 18 hours for inbound and outbound shipments, with members of local meat, textile, and electronics industries also reporting ground transportation disruptions.  

Expert testimony to media suggests that the cause of the strike was a critical failure in judgment by Transnet managers. Historically, Transnet has announced incentive bonus payments on the morning that financial statements are released to the public. Such an announcement was anticipated at the end of June and it is understood that employees were under the impression that bonus payments would be processed at that time in a regular fashion. However, the financial statement release has been delayed by an ongoing audit that is not likely to be concluded until mid- August, and Transnet is not able to disburse the funds until the audit is completed. 

As the end of June neared, with funds for bonus payment disbursal inaccessible until the audit is completed, Transnet managers issued a new stipulation that bonus payments will be paid to employees on the condition that employees have met on-time-performance targets, a proposal that was reportedly rejected by some workers. While labor unions representing Transnet employees chose not to resort to industrial action, non-unionized workers expressed frustration at the handling of the matter and organized their own strike. As evidence of their frustration, this action was executed without sanctioning from South African courts, which protects employees from being fired for strike participation.  At least 11 employees have been suspended for their participation. 

On July 14, Transnet announced that it has obtained an interdiction from the Labor Court of Port Elizabeth that orders striking employees to halt their action. Reports on July 15 indicated that performance at Transnet Port Terminals was already improving. Delays are likely to persist as backlogs are cleared.

Headline: USGS reports magnitude 6.3 earthquake 4km southeast of Calatagan, Batangas Province
Details:

There has not been a tsunami warning issued and there are no immediate reports of damages, though they are possible due to the intensity of the tremor.
USGS (United States Geological Survey) is a scientific agency of the U.S. government which monitors earthquake activity worldwide. USGS earthquake alerts are assessed primarily using the moment magnitude (Mw) scale. However, local magnitude (ML), surface-wave magnitude (Ms) or body-wave magnitude (Mb) may be used in lieu of the Mw scale. All magnitude scales should yield approximately the same value for any given earthquake.

Headline: Peru   Updated reports indicate the strike has been called off after negotiations. Incident closed.
Details:
Truck drivers affiliated with the Union of Transporters and Logistics (GTL) staged a nationwide strike across Peru. Updated reports indicate the strike has been called off after successful negotiations on Saturday. The strike was called to demand a reduction in tolls and taxes on diesel, as well as a solution to alleviate vehicular congestion at the port of Callao. Union representatives claimed that at least 40,000 truckers participated in the labor action across the country. Media sources reported that at least 200 fuel transporters joined the labor action on Thursday, which threatened to cause fuel supply shortages in the northern regions of Lambayeque, Piura, Cajamarca, La Libertad, San Martin, and Amazonas. In addition, the strike caused supply chain disruptions to the distribution of important commodities, such as cement, sugar, rice, and other agricultural products. 

Truck drivers that participated in the labor action utilized their tractor-trailers to block intercity highways in multiple locations throughout the country. At least one roadblock was reported in the southern region of Arequipa along Highway 115. As a result of the roadblocks in Arequipa, at least 30 public transportation companies, including inter-provincial bus services, suspended ticket sales across the region as a safety precaution for travelers. Authorities requested that bus companies suspend ticket sales to various southern regions, including Lima, Ica, and Tacna.  Local news outlets reported other blockades were erected along the Panamericana Norte Highway, preventing the transportation of dairy products and other goods from Cajamarca, Chiclayo, and Trujillo southward to Lima. Furthermore, media sources reported that up to 60 thousand tons of goods were effectively stranded at the port of Salaverry, in the northern region of La Libertad. Five maritime vessels were unable to unload their cargo at the port due to the backlog. Expect residual disruptions as cargo transportation returns to normal. This incident is closed.

Headline: Congestion issues causes higher costs and diversions at Port of New York/New Jersey
Details: Industry sources on February 27 indicated that shipping liners have recently taken measures to reduce delays caused by the ongoing congestion issues in the Port of New York/New Jersey. The congestion has been ongoing since the beginning of the year due to shortage in available labor, inclement weather and an unexpected volume surge. Maersk subsidiary APM Terminals has reportedly taken measures including diverting vessels to other facilities within the port, such as Port Newark Container Terminal, through the end of February 2019. In addition, significant import rail volumes are being barged on a weekly basis from APM New York to Norfolk and loaded on the rail for on-carriage inland. No demurrage is being charged on import rail-boxes which are delayed. Additional labor is being hired, handling equipment has been added and gates will continue to be open on the weekends.

Headline: Congestion issues at Port of Southampton deteriorate as ocean carriers omit calls - UPDATE 2
Details:
Shipping sources report on December 8 that amid worsening congestion issues at the Port of Southampton, THE Alliance has announced it will cancel calls at the port for its vessels NYK Deneb and CMA CGM Kerguelen. The port has faced issues of bad weather, vessel delays and a customs software shutdown in the last few days, resulting in failed deliveries and an increase in backlogs. 
Previously, ocean carriers announced they would impose congestion surcharges on cargo shipped to and from the Port of Southampton due to the congestion. Hapag-Lloyd previously announced a surcharge of EUR 175 per TEU for cargo from Far East Asia to London Gateway from November 15. In addition, CMA CGM will impose a surcharge of USD 100 per TEU for cargo from and to Australia and New Zealand from November 30 and from and to the Indian subcontinent, the Middle East and the Red Sea from November 15. It will also impose a surcharge of USD 150 per TEU for cargo from North East and South East Asia, China, Hong Kong and Macao to Southampton from November 15.

Headline: Piracy Increases in the Singapore Strait; Two Incidents Reported on Friday
Details:
On Friday, two vessels were attacked by suspected pirates in the Singapore Strait. The first incident targeted a tanker, while a bulk carrier was targeted less than two hours later. In both instances, crew were tied up but the pirates were able to escape. No significant losses were reported. In the first boarding, three pirates were sighted, while six were reportedly involved in the second boarding. 

Assessment: Since the start of the year, there have been 29 piracy incidents reported in the Straits of Malacca and Singapore (SOMS) area. This is a significant increase from the eight incidents that were reported in 2018. While the exact reason for the increase is unknown, it is possible that a new criminal group is operating in the area. The number of incidents is still much lower than the peak of piracy in the region in 2015, which saw 96 incidents. However, the relatively high numbers so far this year could be a sign that piracy is becoming a more serious problem in the SOMS area. Customers with supply chains traveling through the region should be aware of the increase of piracy incidents and consider having vessels heighten their vigilance and take other security precautions as appropriate.

Headline: Dockworkers protest against driverless trucks at Port of Los Angeles
Details: Local media sources reported that hundreds of union dockworkers with the Port of Los Angeles turned out for a protest Tuesday (April 16, 2019) morning against the use of automated trucks at one of its terminals. During a brief but packed meeting, the L.A. Board of Harbor Commissioners unanimously voted to table a decision on whether to approve a permit which would allow the Dutch company APM to use driverless cargo vehicles at its Pier 400 terminal. The five-member board decided to delay the vote in response to a letter from L.A. Mayor Eric Garcetti. The vote was followed with boos and jeers from the crowd as the approximately 5-minute meeting was quickly brought to an end. Since APM requested the permit back in September of 2018, the issue has prompted several demonstrations from Port of L.A. dockworkers who fear the introduction of driverless vehicles at Pier 400 will begin a slippery slope that will lead to the loss of thousands of jobs at both the Port of L.A. and the Port of Long Beach.

Headline: U.S. Consulate General in Tijuana Issues Weather Alert Regarding Tropical Storm Lorena
Details:
On Thursday night, the U.S. Consulate General in Tijuana issued the following Weather Alert for American citizens in Mexico:

 Location: Mexican State of Baja California Sur

Event: Mexico has issued a hurricane warning for the Baja California peninsula from La Paz to Santa Fe, and a hurricane watch along the east coast of the Baja California peninsula from north of La Paz to San Evaristo, and along the west coast of the Baja California peninsula from north of Santa Fe to Puerto Cortes. A tropical storm warning remains in effect from Manzanillo, Colima to Punta Mita, Michoacan. Tropical storm Lorena is forecast to re-strengthen into a hurricane and move very close to the southern portion of the Baja California peninsula by Friday afternoon, and could bring hurricane conditions to the area. Heavy rains, strong winds, and heavy surf are expected, which could cause life-threatening flash floods and mudslides.

Protecci n Civil for Baja California Sur announced all schools will be closed on September 20 and port activities are currently restricted. Protecci n Civil has reassured the public there are adequate supplies of food, water, and gas. At present, Consulate General Tijuana has received no reports of flight cancelations and the Mexican government has not published lists of shelters.

The Consular Agency in Los Cabos will remain available for emergency inquiries tomorrow, September 20.  Consulate General Tijuana continues normal operations.

Actions to Take:
 Monitor the U.S. National Hurricane Center, the Mexican National Meteorological Service (Servicio Meteorol gico Nacional), and your local Mexican Civil Protection Agency ( Protecci n Civil ) for updates on storm activity and emergency response.
 Monitor the local news for updates, follow directions from local officials, and in case of emergency call 911.
 Enroll in the Smart Traveler Enrollment Program (STEP) to receive safety messages and other travel information.
 Visit the Department of State s Hurricanes, Typhoons, and Cyclones page for more information. 

To view the Weather Alert in its entirety, please refer to the following URL: https://mx.usembassy.gov/weather-alert-tropical-storm-lorena-sep-19-2019/.

Headline: Salvage completion on Long Tau River delayed to February 2020 - UPDATE 3
Details:
Updated sources indicate that salvage operations of the VietSun Integrity have been temporarily suspended on the Long Tau River due to a major diving incident. The estimated timeline for completion of the operations has been postponed to February 2020. A channel waterway with draft restrictions of 10m has been arranged as an alternative route to Cat Lai Port. Vessels with drafts exceeding 10m have been allowed to pass on a case-by-case basis. 

Previous reporting in October 2019 indicated the following information:  

Cargo vessels with port calls at Cat Lai Container Terminal in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam are facing disruptions in freight movement and restrictions on capacity due to delays in vessel schedules after Long Tau River was closed temporarily on October 19 as a result of a maritime accident. 
VietSun Integrity, a domestic vessel, was carrying 285 unspecified containers with 17 crew members onboard when it started to list and later sank at around 01.30 (local time) on October 19, shortly after leaving the port. Although all crew members were rescued, the containers as well as the ship sank within two hours after the initial distress signal was issued. 

Marine traffic suspended
In response, Ho Chi Minh City Port authorities have temporarily suspended all marine traffic from the junction of the Dong Tranh - Long Tau River for an indefinite period and all vessels to Cat Lai have been directed to use Soai Rạp channel as an alternative route. The closure allows time to clean up 150 tons of spilled oil as well as to recover the lost containers and the ship. 

While initial reports suggested that the closure may last for up to 3 or 4 weeks, local sources on October 30 indicated that it may be extended for up to 100 days or 3 months as the salvage operation is expected to take longer. This is reportedly because the sunken ship may need to be segregated into 20 pieces with a crane. As of October 28, 63 containers have been found, about 42m3 of oil has been collected, and buoys have been placed around the accident site to prevent the oil from spreading further. 

Impact to cargo movement

The average waiting time for vessels at Cat Lai port is currently around 1.5 to 2 days with reports suggesting that marine traffic near the affected site has slowed down. Ships are also facing an increase in fuel costs due to the longer distance that need to be traversed via the Soai Rap River. Moreover, carriers are also being forced to reduce cargo capacity as the river’s depth is shallower than Long Tau River’s. 
At present, the maximum cargo capacity for carriers using the river is at 30 percent with the maximum draft restriction for vessels at 9 meters. Vessels with drafts that are above 9 meters have been directed to Cai Mep International Container Terminal, mainly used for export and import of agricultural products. As the draft restrictions limit vessels in their cargo loading capacity, some shipping lines have reportedly reduced freight at other international ports in order to have enough draft to bypass the route and to pick up goods at Cat Lai Port. As a result, carrier operations and port schedules have been impacted, especially during the peak period of import and export season, as the year is coming to an end. 

The Vietnam Maritime Administration has requested import and export enterprises to provide services at ports in Ho Chi Minh City, Vung Tau, and Dong Nai to ease difficulties for carriers. Cat Lai is the biggest container terminal in Ho Chi Minh City's port area, and is mostly used to ship containers to and from the industrial areas of Ho Chi Minh City. Everstream Analytics customers with shipments to Cat Lai are advised to liaise with local carriers and consider cargo offloading and loading options at Cai Mep - Thi Vai Port to avoid the draft restrictions. However, delays in pickup and delivery services and changes to port calls on short notice can be expected at least until the Long Tau River reopens.

Headline: Reports of More than 20 Ships Transporting Australian Coal Waiting for Months to Unload in China
Details:
According to recent media reports, there are at least 21 ships transporting Australian coal that have been waiting for a month or longer to unload at the Port of Jingtang in Tangshan, southeast of Beijing. Of those anchored off the coast, 15 have been waiting to dock since June. The delays come following reports last month that Chinese authorities had ordered some utilities to stop importing Australian coal. Approximately 400 sailors are onboard the ships off Jingtang, along with up to two million tons of coal. China also officially suspended imports of timber from the Australian state of Victoria this week due to bark beetles having been discovered in previous shipments. A similar ban on timber from Queensland took effect earlier this month.



Assessment: Several of the coal freighters waiting to unload at Jingtang have Indian crew members, and their shipboard conditions have drawn the attention of the Indian government. The Jag Anand, owned by Mumbai-based Great Eastern Shipping, has been waiting to berth since June, with 23 Indian crew aboard, while another ship, the Anastasia, has 18 Indian crew members. The Chinese foreign ministry on Friday denied reports that the Jag Anand has been restricted from departing China, blaming the ship’s operator for not wanting to change its itinerary for financial reasons. Great Eastern Shipping has claimed that it has tried to send the ship on to Japan for a crew change but has been unable to due to unspecified reasons. The crew is unable to disembark in China because of COVID-19 restrictions. The Indian Embassy in China is in contact with the Hebei provincial government over the ship’s situation, and the Australian government has also reached out to Chinese authorities in relation to the ship. According to the International Transport Workers’ Federation (ITF), some of the sailors on the Jag Anand have been on board for nearly two years, while the National Union of Seafarers of India has described the ships waiting off Jingtang as “floating prisons.” There is the potential for labor action in solidarity with the confined sailors, although nothing has been immediately announced. 



The directions last month from Chinese authorities to halt Australian coal imports were reportedly delivered verbally and there has still been no official indication from the government of a direct block on coal from Australia. The Australian government, however, has reported a sharp drop in demand from China for coal over the past month, and some Australian shipments have been diverted to other markets. As for the block on timber shipments due to bark beetles, Australian officials have acknowledged concerns over how effective pest fumigation is on timber from trees that were affected by last season’s wildfires, and have stated that they are cooperating with China on the issue. This would seem to indicate that the ban is a legitimate issue for China to raise, even if it fits nicely with current economic measures being taken against Australia as relations between the two countries remain low. Tensions between Australia and China are likely to deteriorate further as coal shipments remain delayed, while China-India relations could also take another hit if the sailors waiting on the ships become more of a high-profile humanitarian issue. Those with interests that might be impacted by the ongoing frictions in these national relationships are advised to remain abreast of developments.

Headline: Philippine Coast Guard Increasing Patrols Around Ports of Manila, Batangas Following Robbery Reports
Details:
On Thursday, Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) officials announced that patrols and intelligence-gathering operations are being increased in the vicinity of the Ports of Manila and Batangas due to a recent rise in shipboard robberies reported by the Singapore Navy. As part of the initiative, offshore surveillance will be increased in the Bay of Manila and along the coast of southern Luzon. PCG personnel will increase the number of boarding operations of suspicious vessels carried out in the region, especially overnight. The PCG is also coordinating with local governments and law enforcement on the measures.



Assessment: The reported rise in robberies comes as the Philippine government has been promoting the use of the country’s ports as crew-change locations. According to the Singapore Navy, most of the recent robberies have been carried out by suspects entering docked ships via climbing, either from the shore or from small boats. Suspects have then used knives to threaten people on board the ships, absconding with equipment and other objects. There have been no initial reports of serious injuries in the recent incidents. PCG officials have stated that they had received reports of recent burglaries of items from ships, but no armed robberies. Those utilizing shipping in the region are advised to maintain strong security precautions on board ships, and to expect an increased coast guard and police presence in and around the Ports of Manila and Batangas.

Headline: Customs officials seize 242 kg of cocaine in containers at Port of Rotterdam
Details: Dutch media sources on July 24 reported that customs officers working at the Port of Rotterdam found two different shipments concealing a total of 242 kilograms of cocaine, worth EUR 18 million (USD 21,15 million). Both shipments were discovered in containers, beginning with a batch of 30 kilograms found in a sea container filled with the pulp of oranges. The citrus product was destined for a Rotterdam company, and had arrived on a vessel which departed from Santos, Brazil. The cocaine was found hidden behind a wall inside the container. The much bigger load of 212 kilograms of the drug was found in a container filled with printer ink. The shipment was to be delivered to a company in Germany, after arriving in Rotterdam from Paranagua, Brazil. The drugs were found inside 11 duffel bags stuffed in the sea container.

Headline: Explosion Targets Oil Tanker at Port of Jeddah, Highlighting Vulnerability to Commercial Shipping
Details:
No injuries were reported following an explosion that targeted an oil tanker at the Saudi Arabian Port of Jeddah early on Monday, December 14. According to Saudi sources, the British-owned, Singapore-flagged tanker, BW Rhine, was reportedly targeted by a bomb-laden boat at approximately 12:40 AM local time, causing an explosion and a fire. Although the ship’s crew and firefighters reportedly extinguished the fire, the attack caused damage to the tanker’s body, though there are no concerns as of this writing of an oil spill. Reports also indicated that the attack shut down Jeddah port, though as of now, it remains unclear if operations have resumed. The BW Rhine had docked at Jeddah on December 12, carrying over 65,000 tons of gasoline from an Aramco refinery at Yanbu for consumption in the Kingdom. Following the attack, the United Kingdom Marine Trade Operations issued an advisory, stating that an investigation has been opened, and urging all ships in the area to exercise caution. The attack has not yet been claimed by any group. 



Assessment: The incident underscores the vulnerability of Saudi Arabia’s oil infrastructure, and highlights risks posed to commercial shipping in the Red Sea. The explosion also marks the fourth such assault targeting Saudi energy infrastructure in a month. Most recently, a mine exploded off the coast of Shuqaiq and damaged a Maltese-flagged oil tanker on November 25, in an attack claimed by Houthi rebels. Although Saudi officials have not blamed anyone for the most recent attack on December 14, bomb-laden boats and limpet mines have been used periodically by Houthi rebels in the past, suggesting the Shia militia was likely responsible. Saudis typically claim to intercept and destroy unmanned, bomb-laden boats; however, any damage to commercial vessels in this region has the potential to damage production facilities, possibly affecting supply chains and oil prices, as the Red Sea is a vital shipping lane for international energy supplies and other cargo. Headline: Pirates Kidnap Three from Tanker in Gulf of Guinea; Highlighting High Threat from Piracy
Details:
Earlier this week, sources reported that pirates kidnapped three crewmembers from a tanker in the Gulf of Guinea. Details on the incident remain scarce and disputed; however, the Stelios K tanker reportedly went dark on November 16 either off the coast of Lagos, Nigeria or Lome, Togo. The vessel is believed to have been boarded by pirates who remained onboard until at least November 19. The vessel has since been located and three crewmembers have been reported missing. The Nigerian Navy is searching for the attackers, but no arrests have immediately been reported.



Assessment: The incident brings the total number of kidnappings in the Gulf of Guinea to at 23 so far this year, including 10 in November alone. It also brings the total number of crewmembers kidnapped to nearly 120. While kidnappings remain common in the Gulf of Guinea and are often carried out by piracy groups to secure ransom payments, there have been some suggestions that the latest incident may instead have been related to a business dispute. Regardless, the incident has highlighted the high threat from piracy across the Gulf of Guinea, particularly during the dry season, which generally runs from November to March. Due to the high threat from pirates, all nonessential travel in the Gulf of Guinea should be avoided. Those continuing to operate in the area are urged to exercise a high level of vigilance at all times and ensure that appropriate security measures are in place to deter potential attackers.

Headline: Likely collapse of Yemen's Hodeidah ceasefire and government offensive...
Details: (FIRST PUBLISHED 19 MARCH 2019)The Houthi movement announced at a news conference in Sanaa on 16 March that its forces would strike Riyadh and Abu Dhabi with ballistic missiles if the implementation of the United Nations (UN)-sponsored peace deal in the port city of Hodeidah was breached. The Houthis claimed to have intelligence that the internationally recognised Yemeni government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia and the UAE, is preparing to resume its offensive on the port city. The Hodeidah ceasefire came into force on 18 December 2018, but there has since been no progress on implementation of a joint withdrawal from the city. Saudi Arabia and the UAE are reportedly now insisting that they are no longer willing to wait.Significance: IHS Markit assesses that the fundamental disagreement between the Houthis and the government over who will provide the 'local forces' to provide security in Hodeidah after a withdrawal is unlikely to be resolved peacefully, and that the UN-sponsored ceasefire is very likely to collapse in the coming weeks. Should this be the case and a government offensive to recapture the city goes ahead, there would be a severe risk of indiscriminate property damage in the city and the adjacent port from Saudi-led coalition airstrikes and shelling, and protracted urban warfare. Faced with the loss of Hodeidah, the Houthi movement would most likely destroy port facilities and deploy sea mines, making the port unusable for at least several months, and resume missile and IED attacks against coalition shipping in the Red Sea. An indicator signalling an imminent government offensive would be an intensification in shelling of Hodeidah's southeastern neighbourhoods. An agreement by both sides to further face-to-face talks on a specific date would at least temporarily reduce the likelihood of a government offensive. In the event of a government offensive, Houthi retaliation would probably also involve the launch of 'Scud'-type missiles and unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) strikes at military and infrastructure targets against Saudi Arabia, although their impact would be mitigated by Saudi Patriot air defences. Houthi UAVs are unlikely to have the range to strike targets in the UAE, despite a claimed UAV attack.Risks: Civil war, TerrorismSectors or assets affected: Marine, Ground cargo                    Content provided by IHS Markit Foresight © 2019

Headline: Oil Tanker Reported “Hijacked” in Strait of Hormuz, Reflecting Persistent Risk of Maritime Incidents
Details:
Reports from July 15 indicated that an oil tanker was hijacked on July 5 off the coast of the United Arab Emirates. It was not immediately clear what happened aboard the Dominica-flagged MT Gulf Sky, as the tanker’s tracker had been turned off around 4:30 AM local time on July 5, though satellite photos showed the vessel in Iranian waters on July 14, off the coast of Hormuz Island. The ship’s captain reported that two of the ship’s sailors are currently in Tehran, while the twenty-six other crew members returned to India. The tanker had previously been positioned near Khor Fakkan, a city on the eastern coast of the United Arab Emirates (UAE), for months, after the US had accused the ship’s Iranian buyers of attempting to purchase the vessel in coordination with the US-sanctioned National Iranian Oil Company, National Iranian Tanker Company, and the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) Quds Force. It remains unclear how the tanker was able to leave the shores of the UAE after being seized by local authorities. No government officials have yet commented on the incident. 



Assessment: The incident stands to aggravate tensions between the US and Iran in the Gulf region. Although Tehran has appeared to scale back incidents of harassment and other provocative activities around the Strait of Hormuz, following an uptick in such incidents last summer, low-level attacks on tankers using limpet mines and incidents of detaining oil vessels have routinely been blamed on Iran. Most recently, a Hong Kong-flagged oil tanker in the Strait of Hormuz was briefly seized on April 14, allegedly by Iran’s IRGC. Lingering tensions between Washington and Tehran leave open the possibility of further contentious encounters, especially considering that the latest seizure of the MT Gulf Sky represents a possible violation of US sanctions. Tankers in the Persian Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz, and the Bab al Mandeb Strait continue to be targets as part of Tehran’s efforts to push back against the US, which could potentially result in the indiscriminate detentions of civilian vessels.

Headline: COTP for Delaware Bay declares Port Condition WHISKEY
Details:
Industry sources and government announcements indicate the Captain of the Port (COPT) for the Delaware Bay region has declared Port Condition WHISKEY in anticipation of gale force winds, increased seas, surf, coastal flooding, tidal surge and extremely low tides. Such conditions will likely cause delays for all marine cargo and port activity in Delaware. The declaration applies to all Delaware and New Jersey coastlines and intracoastal waters. Port Condition WHISKEY is usually declared by COPTs in anticipation of such weather within 72 hours; ports remain open to traffic for the time being, but all vessels in the area must report their intentions to remain in port or depart within 12-hours of the arrival of gale-force winds.     

The COPT published the following additional requirements for vessels in the area: Vessels must have effective mooring and anchorage arrangements for anticipated high wind; vessel agents are asked to notify vessel masters of this requirement. Facilities must minimize debris that could become missile hazards. Lightering, bunkering, and cargo operations must cease when sustained winds exceed 40 mph.

Headline: Iowa Continuing to Report Significant Damage and Disruptions Following Last Week’s Derecho Event
Details:
Following a severe storm last Monday, communities across Iowa continue to report disruptions and damages. The storm, also known as a derecho, caused winds of almost 100 miles per hour, equivalent to a Category 2 hurricane. Cedar Rapids, the second biggest Iowa city by population, was one of the hardest-hit areas, in the central and eastern portions of the state. Eyewitness accounts in Cedar Rapids have described significant destruction with the majority of structures suffering damage and numerous local roads deemed impassable. An estimated 8,200 homes were damaged in the derecho across the state of Iowa. At least four deaths, three in Iowa and one in Indiana, have been blamed on the storm, which also caused widespread damage across the rest of the Midwest after moving east through Iowa. Upwards of two million people across the region lost power, including at least 600,000 in Iowa. 



In response to the storm, President Donald Trump approved a federal disaster declaration for Iowa that allowed for federal disaster aid for the state. In addition, Governor Kim Reynolds issued a disaster proclamation for 25 counties. The counties included: Audubon, Benton, Boone, Cass, Cedar, Clarke, Clinton, Dallas, Greene, Grundy, Guthrie, Hardin, Iowa, Jackson, Jasper, Johnson, Jones, Linn, Madison, Marshall, Muscatine, Polk, Poweshiek, Scott, Story, Tama, and Washington. In addition, the National Guard was deployed to Linn County to assist in recovery efforts there. Due to the extensive damage in the greater Cedar Rapids area, nightly curfews are currently in effect for Cedar Rapids, Belle Plain, and Tama. 



Assessment: While the majority of the Midwest has had power restored since last week, at least 65,000 people in Iowa, mainly in Linn County, remain without power as of this writing. Officials have warned some of the most hard-hit areas may remain without power for several more days due in part to the fact that thousands of miles of power lines were torn down and several thousand utility poles were damaged beyond repair. Linn County has also reported extensive telecom and internet outages in addition to the power outages. 



The storm has also caused widespread destruction to Iowa farmland, with an estimated several billion dollars in damages. Initial estimates from the U.S. Department of Agricultural (USDA) suggest at least 37.7 million acres of farmland were impacted across the Midwest, including at least 14 million in Iowa. The Iowa damage includes an estimated 8.18 million acres of corn and 5.64 million acres of soybeans, upwards of 43 percent of the state’s total crop. Farmers with affected crops have been advised to file loss claims immediately; however, officials have stated exceptions will be made to the rule requiring farmers to file such claims within 72 hours due to the ongoing power and telecom disruptions. Corn and soybeans represent a major part of Iowa’s economy, roughly $10 billion. Damage assessments remain ongoing and it remains to be seen whether any of the damaged crops are salvageable. While the damaged crops are a major part of the Iowa economy, it is not expected that crop loss significantly impacts the price and availability of those products for U.S. consumers. 



Derechos most often occur during the months of June, July, and August and typically impact the central and eastern regions of the United States; however, they are much rarer compared to regular or severe thunderstorms. To be classified as a derecho, a storm much produces winds of at least 57.5 miles per hour over a path at least 250 miles long and has no more than three hours separating individual wind reports. These types of storms move extremely quickly, often between 50 to 70 miles per hour, allowing them to cause damage over extensive portions of land. The storms often form with little to no warning and the Iowa derecho left residents with as little as 30 to 45 minutes to prepare for the storm. This was the second derecho of 2020 after the first traveled through Ohio, Pennsylvania, New Jersey, and West Virginia at the beginning of June. That derecho also caused widespread damage, killing four people and leaving upwards of a million people without power. Due to the widescale damage these events can cause, the public is advised to always heed severe weather warnings from local authorities and seek shelter immediately. Those with interests in Iowa are advised to use caution due to the amount of storm debris remaining and continue monitoring developments related to the storm.

Headline: Vietnam bans scrap import to keep its ports congestion-free
Details:
Since May 2018, major ports in Vietnam such as Cat Lai Port and Hai Phong Port have faced severe congestions due to high volume imports of containers filled with paper, plastic and metal scrap materials. The congestion in Vietnamese ports may partially be the result of China’s ban on scrap imports since early 2018, prior to which, it used to allow half of the world’s plastic waste into the country. Due to the new environment policies adopted by China, many waste export businesses were left to find new emerging markets such as Southeast Asia to import their scrap materials. One country in particular is Vietnam, where waste import had increased since China’s ban. Sources indicate that the United States is the largest importer of scrap into Vietnam with around 147 million pounds of plastics imported between January and May 2018. This reflects an increase of about 85 million pounds from 2017 and 56 million pounds from 2016 respectively. 

In May, port operating companies and customs offices experienced capacity constraints with containers being left at ports for more than 30 to 90 days. In Cat Lai Port alone, there were about 8,050 TEUs of long-day stored goods, 5,234 TEUs of plastic and waste-paper materials and a remaining 2,816 TEUs of goods that were being stored for 90 days or longer. As a result, many imported goods were left in queue at Cai Mep and Tan Cang– Hiep Phuoc Ports before they were moved to Cat Lai Port, thus creating a ripple congestion effect at other ports. 

This led the authorities to impose a ban on waste imports on June 15. The ports also stopped accepting plastic scrap shipments effective at all ports from June 25 to October 15. The temporary ban not only buys time for the ports to clean up the abandoned containers but also provides an opportunity for the authorities to formulate short and long-term strategies to assess the ports’ storage capacity constraints and its plastic recycling industry. It is evident that for its short-term plan, legislative actions against unlawful imports of scrap would be taken as the port authorities reportedly started cracking down on illegal shipments of paper, plastic and metal scrap by investigating the owners of the containers and those responsible for the illegal imports. 

Furthermore, the port authorities will take the ownership of inspecting permits of imported scrap containers before allowing vessels to unload. Sources indicate that authorities also found companies that were deliberately importing illegal waste under a false name with fake licenses and incorrect addresses to earn quick profits while they leave their trash at the terminals. Hence, ports are now only allowing vessels to unload scrap containers if they have valid import permits and written date commitments to pick up the cargo.

Moreover, legal documents on the management of waste imports will be revised, taking into account environmental protections, and mechanisms to prevent, control & manage the trade and imports of scraps from other countries will be established. Despite these efforts, as of early October 2018, there were still reportedly 4,000 containers of scrap at Cat Lai Port which includes 3,000 containers that had been left for more than three months.

Although the scrap import ban is temporary and is expected to last only for a few months, it is likely that Vietnam will gradually reduce the import of overseas scraps and simultaneously increase the reuse of recycled materials in its long-term strategic approach. Solid waste ban had impacted local recycling industries, as sources suggested that waste processing is an additional source of raw materials for the country’s paper, plastic and steel industries. 

Despite the environmental and port congestion concerns, there is still a demand for overseas paper and plastic scraps for some domestic productions, due to the inadequate plastic recycling system in the country. Sourcing of scrap locally is reportedly difficult as most plastic wastes are normally mixed with regular trash and are not separated properly. Ho Chi Minh City alone produces about 900 tons of plastic waste daily, of which only 90 tons are recycled. While there are pros and cons in the scrap policy, efforts for local recyclers to switch to domestic waste will progress gradually in years to come as the industry needs time to adjust from handling import waste to domestic waste. 

It is not only Vietnam that needs to find a win-win solution for both ports and the domestic recycling industry; Thailand and Malaysia have also followed Vietnam’s footsteps in banning plastic waste due to an increase in such imports. On July 2, Thailand was the second country after Vietnam to ban the import of certain waste goods, including plastic scrap, electronic waste and hazardous waste at Ports of Laemchabang and Songkhla. However, unlike Vietnam, the duration of the ban remains unclear for Thailand. In the same vein, Malaysia has cancelled the import licenses for 114 of the country’s plastic scrap processors and implemented new operating procedures and regulations for recyclable material import licenses. Sources indicated that authorities will conduct inspections to ensure that only processors with valid permits are allow to continue operations. It is also important to note that Indonesia had begun inspecting 100 percent of scrap imports since early April following an increase in imports of scrap polystyrene from the United Kingdom in the first three months of this year. 

As most Southeast Asian nations take a tougher stance on waste import while they struggle with their own domestic waste problems, waste shippers are left with fewer options to find alternative markets to substitute China. It is no doubt that China’s ban has disrupted the global supply chain which had about 7 million tons of scrap plastic imported annually from the United States and Europe. Headline: Dispute around freight rates in Brazil lead to congestion at ports
Details:
The nationwide trucker strikes that swept through Brazil during the last two weeks of May 2018 are continuing to have ripple effects throughout the country. The most recent developments in this regard have been the negotiations between the government and the truckers over minimum freight haulage rates known as the ‘tabela de frete’, or the minimum freight table. The most notable result of this persistent dispute is its effect on sea ports. 
Over the past several weeks, disputes between truckers and shippers have occurred at some of Brazil’s principal ports, such as Santos and Paranagua. This is evident in the backup of cargo at the aforementioned ports, triggered by a dispute between shippers and truckers on what the agreed freight prices are. Shippers claim that the post-strike rates are too high to make shipping affordable. Truckers, on the other hand, claim that the current rates were the best possible concession received during the course of the strike, and any contestation of the rates will lead them back to strike. 
A longer term issue lies with the government setting the definitive price schedule, which it has done so far through a provisional measure. This measure allows ANTT, a national ground transportation entity, to set the freight prices. The Brazilian Supreme Federal Tribunal, the highest court in the country, has heard the arguments posed by both the government and truckers in court on June 28, and is expected to announce its decision on August 27. 
This, however, does not alleviate the immense pressure that the industry will be under pending the decision. The continuing dispute has resulted in freight being stuck at ports, with cargo vessels and containers backed up and unable to move until freight rate disputes are resolved. No similar backlog has been reported in this context at any of the major international cargo airports in the country. The use of air freight as an alternative to circumvent the backlog at the seaports may be considered.
Agribusiness is the most immediately affected industry due to the perishability of the products involved. Until a decision is reached at the Supreme Federal Tribunal in August 2018, customers with cargo at Brazilian seaports are advised to keep abreast of new developments and, where appropriate, explore alternatives.

Headline: COTP for Delaware Bay (including NJ) declares Port Condition WHISKEY
Details:
Industry sources and government announcements indicate the Captain of the Port (COPT) for the Delaware Bay region has declared Port Condition WHISKEY in anticipation of gale force winds, increased seas, surf, coastal flooding, tidal surge and extremely low tides. Such conditions will likely cause delays for all marine cargo and port activity in New Jersey. The declaration applies to all Delaware and New Jersey coastlines and intracoastal waters. Port Condition WHISKEY is usually declared by COPTs in anticipation of such weather within 72 hours; ports remain open to traffic for the time being, but all vessels in the area must report their intentions to remain in port or depart within 12-hours of the arrival of gale-force winds.     

The COPT published the following additional requirements for vessels in the area: Vessels must have effective mooring and anchorage arrangements for anticipated high wind; vessel agents are asked to notify vessel masters of this requirement. Facilities must minimize debris that could become missile hazards. Lightering, bunkering, and cargo operations must cease when sustained winds exceed 40 mph.

Headline: Wind Event to Impact Southern CA This Week; Dangerous Wildfire Conditions and PSPS Events Possible
Details:
Meteorologists are predicting a new round of Santa Ana winds affecting Southern California this week. Winds are expected to gradually increase all week and winds of up to 65 miles per hour are possible by the end of the week in Los Angeles and Ventura counties. The high winds in combination with humidity in the single digits and no expected precipitation may create dangerous fire conditions. Though no warnings have been issued as of this writing, a Public Safety Power Shutoff (PSPS) event may be implemented at some point this week by Southern California Edison (SCE) to help mitigate the potential risk of a fire sparking due to SCE equipment. 



Assessment: Santa Ana wind events occur when strong winds blow from mountain ranges inland down towards the Southern California coast. These most often occur during the fall months but can extend into December. These wind events often spark some of the most destructive wildfires in Southern California especially when they occur at the same time as extremely dry conditions or above-average temperatures, as will be the case this week. A similar wind event occurred last week and resulted in a PSPS event that led to over 8,000 SCE customers temporarily losing power on Thanksgiving Day; however, no significant fires spread during that event. 



Though December is past peak wildfire season, California is still susceptible to destructive fires due to the wind events. In December 2017, the Thomas Fire burned over 281,000 acres in Ventura and Santa Barbara counties, making it at the time the largest fire in California history, and the rapid spread of the fire over an initial five-day period was blamed on a Santa Ana wind event. That fire destroyed over 1,000 structures and led to the evacuation of hundreds of thousands of residents. Additionally, the cause of the fire was found to be SCE equipment. Due to the potential for quick-spreading and potentially dangerous fires, businesses and residents in Southern California are advised to review and/or create emergency plans and evacuation routes. Cal Fire has created guidance on emergency wildfire plans that can be viewed at the following link: https://www.fire.ca.gov/media/4996/readysetgo_plan.pdf. Moreover, residents and businesses should prepare for potential prolonged power outages in the event of PSPS events implemented by SCE. Details on any potential events can be viewed at the following site: https://www.sce.com/wildfire/psps. Heed all instructions from local authorities.
Category: Weather Advisory, Hazmat Response, Network Disruption

Headline: 7,000 tons of cargo bound to Galapagos Islands stuck in Puerto Gal in Guayaquil

Headline: UPDATE - USA: Weather warnings issued in south east Texas due to Tropical Depression Imelda; flooding expected

Houston's police chief has warned of a significant potential for flooding and urged people to avoid unnecessary travel. Imelda is forecast to produce total rainfalls of 6 to 12 inches across the upper coastal region of Texas, which includes Houston and Galveston. The National Weather Service in Houston reported Tuesday night that around 7 inches of rain had fallen in some areas. Flash flood watches had been issued for areas with a population of around 6 million people, including in Houston and Galveston.

Headline: Tamil Nadu & Puducherry – Clean-up operations underway following flooding. Event closed. - UPDATE 12
Details:
Clean-up operations are underway across Tamil Nadu and Puducherry after two tropical storms passed through the area and caused flooding. Tropical Storm Nivar was the first storm to strike the area, followed by Tropical Storm Burevi. At least five people were killed from flood-related incidents, while thousands of people were evacuated. An unspecified number of homes were damaged in Puducherry.

At least 2,000 homes were damaged by floodwaters across Tamil Nadu. Areas that were impacted include Thoothukudi, Ramasamypuram, Boltonpuram, Pucklepuram, and Mela Thattaparai. In Chennai, Bagyalakshmi Nagar, Ayyanar Colony, and other areas were inundated with floodwater. The heavy rainfall also filled the Gadana, Ramanadhi, Karupppanadhi, and Adavinainar dams to the maximum limit, causing an overflow of the Uppaaru river and subsequently the Korampallam tank which flooded several fields and the Tiruchendur highway. This event is closed.

Headline: Port of Cape Town issues new instructions over coronavirus outbreak
Details:
Media sources reported that the harbor master at Cape Town has issued instructions due to the coronavirus outbreak:
•	Prior to boarding a vessel, Port Control should be contacted to confirm Free Pratique has been received and enquire about the last three ports of call. Security to also check with ISPS pre-arrival notification.
•	Upon boarding, Health Status of crew to be conformed with the Master.
•	For high risk vessels (those that have been to China, Singapore, South Korea, Taiwan, Thailand, United States potts), boarding officers to wear face mask and gloves.
•	For the warning period, all South African citizens should refrain from consuming foods or liquids on board vessels from high risk areas. Gifts of food should not be accepted.
•	All off port limit crew from affected areas to be carefully screened – no crew to be taken off vessel without Port Health clearance.
•	Port Health declaration also required for all Off Port Limit transfers.
•	Medical evacuations from vessels from affected areas to be screened by Port Health before the person is taken off the vessel.
•	Captain to confirm in writing stowaway sweep was conducted before departing last port. Stowaway search may be requested when alongside, at the vessel’s cost, using specialist companies whose staff have undergone Corona Virus Disease training and/or awareness.
•	Security to inform Port Control of any reported stowaways from vessels calling from affected areas. If reported, vessel must remain at anchor until cleared by Port Health for entry or advised otherwise.
•	Masters must report stowaways on board if vessel calling from an affected area. Vessel to remain at anchor until stowaways are examined and cleared by Port Health or otherwise advised.
•	Strict gangway watches to be maintained at all times.
•	All involved in evacuation of infected crew or stowaways must be trained by Port Health on Corona Virus.
•	Separate lists of vessels calling from Corona-affected areas to be maintained for record purposes.
•	All galley waste of vessels from affected areas to be incinerated and should not be accepted ashore.
•	Additional security to be deployed by the agent for contaminated vessels and no-one to be allowed on board a contaminated vessel except Port Health. Only after clearance can anyone be permitted to enter the vessel.
•	If possible, contaminated vessels should be allocated an isolated berth away from other vessels.
Importers are advised to follow the recommended measures to avoid shipment delays as well as to prevent the virus.

Headline: U.S. Embassy in Tegucigalpa Issues Weather Alert Regarding Hurricane Eta
Details:
On Sunday, the U.S. Embassy in Tegucigalpa issued the following Weather Alert regarding Tropical Storm Eta, which has since strengthened into a Category 1 hurricane on the Saffir-Simpson Wind Scale:



“Location: Honduras



Event:  The Government of Honduras has issued a hurricane watch for areas along the Caribbean coast of Honduras. Tropical Storm Eta is currently approximately 600 kilometers off the coast of Gracias a Dios and is expected to strengthen to a hurricane before it reaches the Caribbean coasts of Central American countries early Tuesday, November 3, 2020.



American citizens in the departments of Gracias a Dios, Atlantida, Colon, Yoro, Cortes, Olancho, and the Bay Islands are advised to prepare for possible inclement weather in the form of storm surge, hurricane-force winds, and heavy rainfall. Heavy rainfall predicted through Thursday, November 5, 2020, may lead to flash flooding and river flooding in affected areas.



American citizens in the departments of Santa Barbara, Comayagua, Francisco Morazan, and El Paraiso are advised to remain alert and continue monitoring weather reports.



Actions to Take: 



• Monitor the National Hurricane Center for updates (https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/).

• Follow guidelines issued by local authorities (http://www.copeco.gob.hn).

• Seek secure shelter.

• Inform a friend or family member of travel plans over the upcoming holiday.

• Have travel documents up to date and easily accessible.

• Prepare an emergency supply kit (ready.gov).

• Notify friends and family of your safety.



Assistance:



U.S. Embassy Tegucigalpa

https://hn.usembassy.gov/

Tel. (504) 2238-5114

USAHonduras@state.gov



State Department – Consular Affairs

888-407-4747 or 202-501-4444”



The Weather Alert can be viewed in its entirety at the following URL: https://hn.usembassy.gov/weather-alert-u-s-embassy-tegucigalpa-honduras-4/.

Headline: UPDATE 26 - 102 miles SSW of Roanoke– Post-Tropical Cyclone Zeta continues to move east-northeast. Event closed.
Details:
Tropical Storm Zeta made landfall as a Category 2 hurricane on the afternoon of Wednesday, October 28 near Concordia, Louisiana. Zeta has since lost tropical characteristics and was declared post-tropical. Post-Tropical Cyclone Zeta continues to move east-northeast at 55 miles per hour, while exhibiting maximum sustained winds of up to 50 miles per hour and higher gusts of 55 miles per hour. Tropical-storm-force winds will continue to extend outward up to 310 miles. Three deaths have been reported thus far; one in Biloxi, Mississippi, a second in New Orleans, Louisiana, and a third in Cherokee County, Georgia. Heavy flooding and wind damage were reported in Louisiana, Mississippi, and Alabama. 

Strong gusts are still possible across portions of eastern North Carolina, southeastern Virginia, and the southern Delmarva Peninsula during the next couple of hours. Moreover, the last of the heavy rainfall along the track of Zeta will impact the Mid-Atlantic through this evening. Additional rainfall totals of an inch or less are expected across these areas, possibly resulting in flash, urban, small stream, and isolated minor river flooding. There are no coastal watches or warnings in effect.

The Tropical Storm Risk has issued a Yellow Alert for Atlantic City, NJ, Salisbury, MD, Kitty Hawk, NC, and Hatteras, NC, currently. Furthermore, a Yellow Alert has been issued for Providence, RI, Boston, MA, New York, NY, Chatham, MA, Montauk, MA, Siasconset, MA, and Belmar, NJ, within nine hours. A Yellow Alert indicates there is a 10–30 percent probability that the storm will result in maximum sustained winds of at least Category 1 strength, or greater than 50 percent probability that it will result in maximum sustained winds of at least tropical storm strength. This event is closed.

Headline: UPDATE - USA: Hurricane Dorian forecast to impact coasts of Georgia and Carolinas, as well as Florida
Details: According to the latest details on 1 September, Hurricane Dorian remains at Category 4 strength as it moves westwards at 8 mph, with maximum sustained winds of 150 mph; just shy of Category 5. Peak winds are predicted to increase to 155 mph. The weather system, previously heading towards Florida's Atlantic coast, is now forecast to target the coasts of Georgia and the Carolinas, where it may approach as a Category 2 system, bringing life-threatening storm surges. The cities of Brunswick, GA; Charleston, SC; and Wilmington, NC, could all see more than six inches of rainfall. A number of Florida’s mandatory evacuation orders have since been postponed, though voluntary requests for evacuations remain across several counties. A significant storm surge and devastating hurricane-force winds are both possible along portions of Florida’s east coast by the early-to-middle part of next week. Even while the majority of computer models predict Dorian to remain just offshore of Florida, officials have warned of significant and potentially devastating impacts. A stretch of Florida's east coast, from Deerfield Beach to Sebastian Inlet, is under a Tropical Storm Watch. Since the storm is predicted to slow down and turn northward as it approaches, the effects from wind, rain and storm surges could be prolonged. Nevertheless, the storm's path could still change and fluctuations in intensity are likely. However, irrespective of the storm’s ultimate course, significant coastal flooding is to be expected.

Headline: Cleanup Operations and Investigation Underway Following Second Recent Oil Spill Near Port Dickson
Details:
Authorities this week discovered a nearly two-mile stretch of oil along a beach at Pantai Cermin, south of Port Dickson. Officials from the Department of Environment (DOE) took samples in an attempt to discover the leak’s origin, and cleanup operations are underway. The affected beach is expected to be closed until at least Friday or Saturday.



Assessment: Although the nature of the Pantai Cermin spill has not been definitively determined, authorities have speculated that it might have come from a passing boat. Some local environmental and economic impact is expected, but officials believe that it will not be very serious. The spill is the second to occur near Port Dickson in a little over a week, following a leak that was detected in the Kampung Gelam area on October 4. That spill, which came from old crude oil pipelines, has since been cleared. Nearby disruptions should be expected while cleanup operations are carried out and an investigation is conducted into the current spill.

Headline: Chinese ports facing operational delays after passage of Mangkhut
Details: Industry sources indicate on September 17 that six Chinese ports continue to be affected by Typhoon Mangkhut, facing closure and anticipated delays until further notice. The Port of Nansha since September 15 is closed and will have a 72 hour delay upon resumption. The Port of Chiwan since September 15 is closed and will have a 72 hour delay upon resumption. The Port of Yantian since September 14 is closed and will have a 72 hour delay upon resumption. The Port of Hong Kong since September 15 is closed and will have a 60 hour delay upon resumption. Headline: Tokyo braces for impact as Super Typhoon Hagibis looms
Details:
After almost one month Typhoon Faxai battered Tokyo metropolitan area in September, the city and its surrounding areas are once again preparing to face an even stronger typhoon on October 12 as it is forecasted to make landfall near Tokyo in the morning. The Category 5 Super Typhoon Hagibis has been termed as “violent” by the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) as the highest classification in the typhoon scale carrying a maximum wind speed of 257 kilometer per hour. 
The typhoon’s intensity is expected to weaken down to a wind speed of 145 kmh by the time it reaches Japan’s shores overnight on October 11-12. Nevertheless, JMA predicts that Hagibis will bring gale force winds, high waves and torrential rain over parts of Honshu, particularly affecting coastal areas that face the Pacific Ocean and Sea of Japan. 
 
Super Typhoon Hagibis projected path over Japan and Everstream Analytics alerts; Source: Everstream Analytics

Port closure
The following seaports have confirmed closures ahead of Typhoon Hagibis. The time periods indicated in the table are approximate local times. Bunker delivery operations at Tokyo Bay and Nagoya have stopped from October 11 until October 15. Bunker prices are unlikely to be affected as suppliers have reportedly made necessary adjustments to their bunker delivery schedules.
