Tokyo 	        Closed	October 11	        October 13, 12:00 or October 14, 05:30
Yokohama	Closed	October 11	        October 13, 12:00 or October 14, 05:30
Chiba	        Closed	October 12	        October 13, 12:00 or October 14, 05:30
Nagoya	       Closed	October 11	        October 13, 12:00 or October 14, 05:30
Kobe	       Closed      October 11, 12:00	October 13, 06:00
Osaka	     Closed	October 11, 12:00 	October 13, 06:00


Airline and rail disruptions
Japan Airlines (JAL) and All Nippon Airways (ANA) have announced cancellation of over 800 domestic flights and 72 international flights via Tokyo’s Narita and Haneda airports from October 11 to 12. Airports that are located along the forecast path of Typhoon Hagibis are likely to face disruptions; these include Nagoya Chubu, Osaka Itami, Osaka Kansai, Sendai airports. Singapore Airlines and EVA airways have also cancelled and rescheduled over 23 international flights to various destinations in Japan scheduled for October 12-13.

Narita is Japan’s top air cargo hub with reported cargo volume of 2.2 million tons in 2018; Kansai and Haneda Airports ranked second and third accordingly. While these airports have not indicated temporary closures on October 12, further flight cancellations may impede air shipments to cause cargo backlog for 24 to 48-hours at least until October 14.   

For rail, fast speed rail services by East Japan Railway Co., Central Japan Railway Co., West Japan Railway Co. will be suspended on October 12 in Hokuriku, Kyoto-Osaka-Kobe, Northern Kinki, San-in and Wakayama lines. JR East operations may also stop both regular and Shinkansen lines in Tokyo area on October 12-13. The Odakyu Electric Railway and Tobu Railway companies will also restrict services in Kanto region. 
Industry Impact 

The projected path of Super Typhoon Hagibis and Typhoon Faxai takes a similar track despite its different intensities. Nevertheless, similar impact can be expected as Tokyo Electric Power Company has warned residents to take measures to prevent blackouts. Everstream Analytics data shows that facilities from four industries are cluttered primarily in Kanagawa prefecture. These include Socionext Inc., chip manufacturer, Mitsui Chemicals, Yorozu Corporation, a manufacturer of automotive and agricultural machinery parts, and Therabiopharma Inc., a biotech firm. Nippon Steel has already announced temporary production halt at its plant in Kimitsu city, Chiba prefecture for safety. The firm has decided to stop blast furnaces and repair works at its plant following infrastructural damages due to Typhoon Faxai. As a result the firm had stopped part of a production line that makes alloy steel materials for automobiles.
 
As the storm’s path as well as its intensity is unpredictable and may change at a short notice, Everstream Analytics customers with sub-tier suppliers based on the path of Super Typhoon Hagibis should prepare for logistical arrangements ahead of the storm. Majority of Japanese manufacturers normally shut down factories for a 24-hour period for safety. However, flooding and power outages are the biggest challenges for manufacturers after the typhoon passage, as inundated roads prevent employees from commuting to business sites and resume productions without appropriate power voltage. In addition, companies are advised to monitor Japan Meteorological Agency for information on weather related warnings as well as to have hurricane preparedness plan on standby to implement when necessary.

Headline: South Africa’s road freight in jeopardy amid xenophobic attacks on foreign drivers
Details:
Cargo trucks driven by foreign nationals in South Africa have faced violent attacks by local truck drivers and other unknown groups since the beginning of the year and the situation has worsened in recent months. The recent attacks escalated after truck drivers affiliated with the National Truck Drivers Founders and All Truck Drivers Foundation (ATDF) issued an ultimatum for foreign truck drivers to vacate their jobs by December 1. This is because South Africans associated with the foundation believe that truck driving is not a specialized skill and can be done by a local driver. Protests against foreign truck drivers have been well-attended in urban centers, and interstate highways and key thoroughfares have been blocked intermittently. 

The anti-foreign sentiment towards foreign truck drivers and their employers in South Africa is not uncommon and the recent unrests associated with the hiring of foreign truck drivers in South Africa are expected to persist over the coming weeks, as the South African National Cargo Transport Drivers Association on December 17 has given 21 days to the National Bargaining Council to deregister all foreign truck drivers. The situation remains fluid, as foreign truck drivers have also threatened to ban South African drivers from entering neighboring countries if they are forced out of their jobs. 

Targeted highways:
Although South Africa’s President Cyril Ramaphosa has condemned the xenophobic attacks, little has been done to protect road freight logistics. Since November 19, 35 cargo trucks have been petrol-bombed. According to media sources, 9 trucks were set alight on the N3 highway during the course of a day, before the foreign drivers were attacked and their cargo looted. Other attacks include vandalism and road blockades with burning tires, making it impassable for vehicles. On November 23, a driver was fatally shot and another injured. The following roads and locations have been targeted since late November: 

•	Kwa Zulu-Natal province: N3, R103, R23, and R550 roads 
•	Free State province: the R59 between Parys and Sasolburg 
•	Gauteng province: N3 in Johannesburg, N12 in Benoni, and R21 in Boksburg 
•	Mpumalanga province: Key routes in Bethal 

In retaliation, foreign truck drivers have threatened to block South African truck drivers from crossing land borders into other neighboring countries, if they are forced to leave their jobs in South Africa. Any such attempts may lead to unrest at cross-border points resulting in congestion or delays for freight trucks and customs processing time, which is already significantly impeded by COVID-19 restrictions. 

Impact on road freight:
South Africa relies heavily on the road freight sector as about 90 percent of freight moves via land transport, particularly the N3 highway that connects between Johannesburg and Durban. It is also used as a key route to transport export and import goods from the Port of Durban to the capital. In recent months, the industry has been hampered by varying disturbances, including traffic congestion at border points, increasing cargo thefts, protests, and violence related to socio-economic issues resulting in road blockades, and mounting storage and demurrage costs on imports and slower freight clearance. In September, cargo trucks faced congestions at South Africa’s border checkpoints with Mozambique, Botswana, and Zambia as protesters against foreign truck drivers and blocked roads. 

Additionally, the South African economy is still reeling from the effects of the COVID-19 lockdowns. When the government imposed a level-5 COVID-19 lockdown in March 2020, local importers had to bear the storage and demurrage cost of around ZAR 1.4 billion (USD 95 million; EUR 77 million) while over 20,000 containers were left in storage facilities, according to the South African Association of Freight Forwarders. While the economy is still at a recovery stage, the recent protests against the hiring of and attacks on foreign truck drivers have caused panic amongst some logistics companies in utilizing their assets and resources, with some haulers having to downsize jobs as trucks stand idle. 

Anti-foreign sentiments:
Demonstrations and attacks against foreign truck drivers are not uncommon in South Africa as there is a widely held perception that trucking companies favor hiring foreign nationals as they accept lower wages. Moreover, the conflict comes at a time of high levels of unemployment amid the economic fallout from the COVID-19 pandemic, fueling xenophobic sentiments across the country. According to the South African Labor Ministry, at least 84 attacks have been registered since April 2020 over the employment of foreign truck drivers. While the ATDF claims that its motive does not stem from xenophobia, precedents indicate that the same type of aggression was directed specifically at foreign drivers and their employers.

Headline: Job Bill Protests Likely to Continue Despite COVID-19 Restrictions; Demonstrations Dispersed Tuesday
Details:
On Monday, Indonesia’s House of Representatives passed a controversial omnibus law on job creation. The legislation, which is intended to spur job creation and lower unemployment by allowing employers more flexibility in hiring decisions, has drawn opposition for revising required severance payments, allowing irregular working hours, and changing the way that minimum wage is calculated. It also removes some tax and environmental regulations for companies. The Confederation of Indonesia Trade Unions and other associations have embarked on a general strike through Thursday in opposition to the bill, with as many as five million people expected to participate. The bill drew largescale protests on multiple occasions in the months before its passage, and demonstrators gathered in various cities across the country on Monday and Tuesday.



Assessment: While the authorities have not explicitly said that protests related to the job law are banned, police officials have stated that large gatherings will remain barred under COVID-19 gathering restrictions. A demonstration against the law that was expected to see up to 5,000 people gather outside the House of Representatives in Jakarta on Monday was largely blocked by police preventing buses carrying protesters from entering the capital. Demonstrators who made it to the protest location were dispersed by officers. On Tuesday, demonstrations were dispersed in at least two cities. In West Java, police used teargas to clear thousands of demonstrators after firecrackers and rocks were thrown and a police vehicle was damaged. At least ten people were arrested. In Banten Province, a demonstration was dispersed with water cannons in Serang. Two police officers at the protest were reportedly injured when rocks were thrown by demonstrators. Authorities have created “cyber patrols” on some social media platforms in order to monitor protest actions, and while additional demonstrations are likely, it is probable that they will face a heavy police response. The Indonesian government has faced previous criticism of using the COVID-19 pandemic to push through controversial pieces of legislation while protest activity can be curtailed. It is advised to avoid the vicinity of any demonstrations due to the risk of escalation.

Headline: Tropical Storm Beta Forms in the Gulf of Mexico Bringing Flooding Threat to the Texas Coast
Details:
Tropical Storm Beta formed in the Gulf of Mexico on Friday and is currently located approximately 360 miles southeast of Corpus Christi, TX. The storm is forecast to meander through the gulf before making a westward turn on Sunday and strengthen into a Category 1 hurricane. Landfall for the storm remains uncertain; however, Beta is expected to move up the Texas coast and could potentially make landfall south of Houston on Tuesday or Wednesday. The National Hurricane Center (NHC) has not issued watches or warnings related to the storm as of Friday afternoon; however, the NHC warned these are likely beginning Friday night or on Saturday. The most up-to-date details on the storm, including path and strength, can be found at the following link: https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/. 



Assessment: Significant uncertainty exists regarding the current path and eventual strength of Beta. Initial estimates suggest that Texas communities along the coast from Brownsville to Houston could see upwards of 12 inches of rain from the storm. Officials have cautioned that the slow-moving nature of Beta could lead to a scenario that just occurred with Hurricane Sally in Florida and Alabama. Sally’s slow movement prior to and during landfall allowed for excessive rainfall with some areas, such as Pensacola, FL, reporting over 25 inches of rain and life-threatening flooding. Though none have been issued as of this writing, evacuations remain a possibility for coastal communities in Texas as the path and strength of the storm become clearer. Due to the potential impacts and uncertainty, those with interests along the Texas coast are advised to closely monitor developments related to Tropical Storm Beta. Emergency plans, potential evacuation routes, and disaster supply kits should be prepared and reviewed.

Headline: IRGC Fires Missiles at Mock US Aircraft Carrier in Show of Force
Details:
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) launched underground ballistic missiles at a replica US aircraft carrier during military exercises in the Strait of Hormuz, near the port city of Bandar Abbas, on July 29. As a result, US troops were reportedly put on alert at the al Dhafra Air Base in Abu Dhabi and the al Udeid Air Base in Qatar. One day prior, the IRGC fired a missile from a helicopter targeting the same fake carrier. Wednesday was expected to be the final day of the maneuvers, in which several units from IRGC’s Navy and Aerospace Division took part. Such military exercises have the potential to result in casualties in cases of mistaken fire, though the maneuvers on July 28 and 29 passed without incident.



Assessment: The incident appears to be geared toward demonstrating Iran’s strength of its missile program, and intimidating US troops in the area. While, an Iranian military commander stated that this was Iran’s first successful attempt to carry out the launch of underground ballistic missiles, the military is known to have vast underground bases hiding its ballistic missile arsenal. In addition to highlighting the country’s network of subterranean projectiles, the military exercises also underline the lingering threat of military conflict between Iran and the US, after a series of escalating incidents last year led to a drone strike in January 2020 that killed Qassem Soleimani, the commander of the IRGC’s Quds Force. Additional incidents, including US officials calling for the UN weapons embargo on Iran, set to expire in October, to be renewed, and an incident on July 23, in which US fighter jets reportedly flew too close to an Iranian passenger plane near Beirut, have also renewed tensions. Despite appearing to heighten tensions, the maneuvers are likely only a show of force designed to intimidate the US, and do not necessarily increase any likelihood of direct confrontation between the rivals.

Several fishermen and their crews have lost jobs and businesses after the permanent withdrawal of recreational fishing vessels permits. Previously, protesters said that they do not intend to block the ports but to sail in their waters and displaying banners.

Headline: Likely collapse of Yemen's Hodeidah ceasefire and government offensive...
Details: Risks: Civil war, TerrorismSectors or assets affected: Marine, Ground cargoThe Houthi movement announced at a news conference in Sanaa on 16 March that its forces would strike Riyadh and Abu Dhabi with ballistic missiles if the implementation of the United Nations (UN)-sponsored peace deal in the port city of Hodeidah was breached. The Houthis claimed to have intelligence that the internationally recognised Yemeni government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia and the UAE, is preparing to resume its offensive on the port city. The Hodeidah ceasefire came into force on 18 December 2018, but there has since been no progress on implementation of a joint withdrawal from the city. Saudi Arabia and the UAE are reportedly now insisting that they are no longer willing to wait.Significance: IHS Markit assesses that the fundamental disagreement between the Houthis and the government over who will provide the 'local forces' to provide security in Hodeidah after a withdrawal is unlikely to be resolved peacefully, and that the UN-sponsored ceasefire is very likely to collapse in the coming weeks. Should this be the case and a government offensive to recapture the city goes ahead, there would be a severe risk of indiscriminate property damage in the city and the adjacent port from Saudi-led coalition airstrikes and shelling, and protracted urban warfare. Faced with the loss of Hodeidah, the Houthi movement would most likely destroy port facilities and deploy sea mines, making the port unusable for at least several months, and resume missile and IED attacks against coalition shipping in the Red Sea. An indicator signalling an imminent government offensive would be an intensification in shelling of Hodeidah's southeastern neighbourhoods. An agreement by both sides to further face-to-face talks on a specific date would at least temporarily reduce the likelihood of a government offensive. In the event of a government offensive, Houthi retaliation would probably also involve the launch of 'Scud'-type missiles and unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) strikes at military and infrastructure targets against Saudi Arabia, although their impact would be mitigated by Saudi Patriot air defences. Houthi UAVs are unlikely to have the range to strike targets in the UAE, despite a claimed UAV attack.                     Content provided by IHS Markit Foresight © 2019

Headline: US Customs and Border Protection issues seaport inspection guidance
Details:
Industry sources indicate on August 3 that the US Department of Customs and Border Protection (CBP) has issued guidance for seaport inspectional processes which will take effect immediately. For cargo ships arriving from COVID-19 travel suspended countries, CBP is delaying the inspection of the crew until 14-days after foreign departure.  The crew remains onboard until inspected.  All vessels will be required to submit a security plan to include the hiring of additional guards for all vessels arriving from suspended countries.  Once the 14-day mark is passed, CBP will inspect the crew and may issue landing permits. In some cases, the ship may depart the port before 14-days and in those cases, the crew is remaining on board for the duration. This applies to vessels and crew arriving from the following countries: 
Iran, China (excluding Hong Kong and Macau), Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Iceland, Italy, Latvia, Liechtenstein, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, United Kingdom, Ireland, and Brazil.

Headline: United Kingdom: Woolwich Ferry to end services in East London until the new year
Details: Services on the free Woolwich Ferry across the River Thames in East London are due to terminate on 6 October until the new year. The Woolwich Ferry links Woolwich and North Woolwich, (near London City Airport), for which a ferry service has been in operation since 1308. The boats are being replaced with more environmental vessels, and the service temporarily discontinued while new berths are built. The final crossings will be made at 19:45 local time on 6 October. Travellers who use the ferry crossing regularly will need to consider alternative routes from 7 October. Note any height and weight restrictions on alternative bridge crossings as necessary.

Details: Media sources on February 27 indicate that China's major container ports have reached a 'turning point' as the cargo backlog begins to loosen after dockworkers, customs officers, tugboat pilots, and other workers have returned to work. According to recent sources, handling times are beginning to improve in the port of Ningo and other Chinese ports, but a shortage of truck drivers bringing containers in and out of the port has caused major bottlenecks. Customers can expect delays and increased waiting times to continue in the coming weeks as the backlogs are gradually reduced.

Flooding has reportedly occurred in the port city of Tamatave. 

As a precautionary measure, the Port of Beira was temporarily closed for navigation and trucks until Thursday, December 31. At least 118 people from the Manicaland district of Zimbabwe were evacuated in preparation of the Chalane. The government established 464 evacuation shelters in preparation of flooding. This event is closed.

Headline: Container terminals close gates in Genoa following bridge collapse; to reopen on August 16
Details:
Transportation and logistics in and around the port city of Genoa have been paralyzed since midday on August 14 after the central span of the Morandi Bridge, a flyover bridge supporting the A10 highway, collapsed onto rail tracks and warehouses. Container terminals at the Port of Genoa, located about 5 kilometers from the bridge, have preemptively closed their gates on August 14, preventing trucks from entering the gates to load or unload containers. Vessel operations were said to continue as usual, and gates are expected to reopen by August 16. 

Road and rail traffic throughout the city of Genoa has already been significantly compromised since August 14. With only one bypass available via the SS1 road and bridge construction works likely taking months before completion, congestion, delays and additional fees will likely affect road, rail and ocean freight transportation from and to Genoa over the coming months. Customers should be mindful of the following transportation impacts when planning shipments to, from or through the Genoa area: 

1.	Cross-terminal movements between the major container terminals VTE and SECH in Genoa, which are linked by the Morandi Bridge, are likely to suffer delays. This is expected to affect export containers in transit, which may miss cut-off times on vessel services. 

2.	Container movements between Genoa and industrial centers such as Torino and Milan in Italy, as well as the French border near Menton, is likely  to experience extended delays as trucks are re-routed via smaller, congested connection roads towards the A12 highway to the north or the A10 highway to the west. 

3.	As rail tracks are likely to remain closed in the short term, potential alternative modes of transportation such as intermodal rail traffic from the Port of Genoa to Milan will also be affected by the bridge collapse. Since containers from Milan are usually connected to Germany through the important Rhine Alpes Rail Corridor via Switzerland, rail exports from factories located in the port area of Genoa are expected to face delays and congestions. Factories in the area include the Ilva steel mill that supplies hot-rolled steel to automotive, packaging and energy customers. 

Customers are advised to monitor recovery efforts in the area and consider the aforementioned impacts to transportation when planning cargo movement in the area.

Headline: UPDATES: Port of Alexandria reopens for vessel entrance & departure
Details: Industry sources indicate on April 2 that the Port of Alexandria is open for vessel entrance and departure again after a March 30 closing due to foul weather. Headline: DAILY BRIEF: Export disruption, cargo delays, and cruises diversion likely...
Details: Risks: Labour strikesSectors or assets affected: Marine; Cargo; Agriculture; TourismOn 27 November 2018, Chile's Finance Minister Felipe Larrain called on for a swift resolution of a workers' strike at the port of Valparaiso that has been ongoing for 11 days. Workers are demanding higher salaries and better working conditions and have paralysed operations. This has forced at least 14 cargo vessels, and three cruise ships to divert to the nearby port of San Antonio, also in Valparaiso region. This has generated increased congestion in San Antonio, which is receiving an additional 500 cargo trucks a day, while ships have to wait for hours to dock. According to port operators' estimates, at least 20,000 containers have been diverted, and losses account for at least USD3.5 million. In 2013â14, three weeks of nationwide port strikes caused losses of approximately USD300 million. The port sector being crucial for Chile's economy, the government has implemented negotiating tables to deactivate the strike.Significance: The strike is likely to continue for several days, as no advances in the negotiations have been reported, causing ground and maritime cargo delays in San Antonio and Valparaiso. Disruption will increase as public-sector unions are also on indefinite strike over minimum-wage demands, likely delaying customs operations. Fruit exports, which use mainly the ports of San Antonio and Valparaiso, will be specifically affected, as the export season begins next week (early December). The diversion of cruises will also undermine Valparaiso's tourism industry, due to a reduction in tourists coming into the city. There is a risk of solidarity strikes in other ports, as members of the Port Union (Union Portuaria) in Antofagasta and Bio Bio regions have supported the strike (but have not announced any action). Statements by union leaders of other ports that they will join the strike will indicate increased risk of nationwide disruption. The strike continuing for longer than a week will indicate significant losses of fruit to be exported, as it is a perishable product, making exporters miss international trade commitments. Headline: Stalled contract negotiations may result in strike or lockout at Port of Montreal
Details: Shipping sources reported this week that dockworkers at the Port of Montreal, Canada, are considering going on strike as talks between port employers and the union have stalled and a labor contract agreement has expired since December 31, 2018. In December, the union voted 99.5 per cent in favour of a strike mandate, which can typically be exercised at any time during contract negotiations, now ongoing. However, earlier this week, a court hearing began and will determine whether the longshoremen can strike or employers can stage a worker lockout if contract negotiations fail. Employers argue that the port should be considered an essential service providing foods and medicine and therefore could not be subject to a strike or lockout. No strikes or lockouts can take place until a decision has been taken. A potential strike may further exacerbate congestion which has affected the port since early 2019.

Headline: Valparaiso terminal workers reject compensation agreement, increasing...
Details: Risks: Labour strikes; Protests and riotsSectors or assets affected: Marine; Cargo; Property; AgricultureOn 19 December, Valparaiso port contractor workers rejected a preliminary agreement mediated by the government to call off a 34-day strike over working conditions and bonuses. The agreement offered them soft loans and other benefits totalling CLP1.37 million (USD1,980), lower than the CLP2 million bonus workers demanded. Confrontations between demonstrators and the police at the port neighbourhood, Colon Avenue, and the city centre, involved protesters erecting barricades using burning tyres, and throwing sticks, stones, and Molotov cocktails at the police, who responded using tear gas and water cannons. Some demonstrators broke windows of nearby property and stores, and looted the offices of maritime company Ultraport. At the union headquarters, approximately 25 individuals threw blunt objects and Molotov cocktails from the roof, which led to the police breaking into the premises and arresting 16 people. Headline: Upper Texas Coast   Recovery efforts are underway in the region; impacts remain. Incident closed.
Details:
While flood waters continue to recede across the eastern coast of Texas, relief and recovery efforts are underway in the region. As a result of flooding caused by the passing of storm Imelda, a total of five people were killed. On Friday, September 20, two bodies were discovered in the Beaumont area, and one was discovered in Houston. There are reports that flood waters have begun to recede in the area, and although rain is in the forecast for the weekend September 28, favorable weather is also predicted. Officials are continuing to survey flooded areas with regard to search and rescue efforts. Governor Greg Abbott declared a state of disaster in 13 counties in response to the severe flooding. The proclamation was for the following counties: Brazoria, Chambers, Galveston, Hardin, Harris, Jasper, Jefferson, Liberty, Matagorda, Montgomery, Newton, Orange, and San Jacinto. There are no immediate reports regarding the current status for each individual county.

The most substantial flooding was reported in Chambers County, specifically in Winnie. In Harris County, the most significant was in Houston, and in Jefferson County, the largest reported flooding was in Beaumont. As of September 25, the only counties under active flood warnings are Jasper, Jefferson and Hardin. Evacuations were issued for residents in Hardin and Jefferson counties. Several other counties were under shelter-in-place orders during the storm and subsequent flooding.

At least ten more inches of rain fell on September 19, with some areas receiving over 15 inches in total. Over three days of rain, the area received at least 50 inches in some locations. A number of chemical and refinery facilities were shut down in the area, including the TC Energy pipeline. The pipeline, which extends from Cushing, Oklahoma to Nederland, Texas, was restarted on Friday, September, 20. Several roadways in the area were deemed impassable due to high water, which may still be present in certain parts.

The following areas were impacted the most by the storm: 

- Chambers County: In Winnie, at least 200 homes were inundated with water and an entire hospital was evacuated. Initial estimates indicated some 800 homes were damaged in the entire county and approximately 400 people were rescued. Although it was closed during the storm, a stretch of I-10 between Beaumont and Winne has since been reopened. There are, however, reports of water on the freeway and only one lane is open.

- Harris County: In Houston, over 1,700 people were rescued, 323 vehicles were reported stranded, and a building collapsed leading to the injury of three people. In Spring, over 100 people were rescued and at least 60 people were rescued in Huffman. Hundreds of homes were inundated in the Humble and Kingwood areas.

- Jefferson County: The County received roughly 40 inches of rain over a 72-hour period. The Green Pond Gulley Levee was at risk of collapse due to deteriorating conditions exacerbated by rainfall. As a result, county officials ordered multiple evacuations as a precaution. The levee is currently in a stable condition. In Beaumont, over 250 high water rescues were performed.

- Galveston County: All Island Transit services were suspended, including fixed routes, Dial-A-Ride, and rubber wheel trolleys. 
As the post-storm process continues, authorities have stated that around 7,000 national flood insurance claims have been made. Expect residual disruptions as water, debris and other associated impacts continue to affect the region. This incident is closed.

Headline: New measures implemented at Port of Salalah amid COVID-19 outbreak
Details:
Media sources reported that additional measures are implemented on March 18 at the Port of Salalah. 
- All ships and their agents are obliged to submit the IMO Declaration of Health to the Harbour Master as well as the attached ‘Coronavirus questionnaire’.
- Both documents should be signed and stamped by the Captain. Both documents need to be uploaded in the Port management system by the ship’s agent for approval of the vessel called by the Harbour Master.
- In case of a sick person on board, the vessel will not be allowed to enter the port and the patient involved will be screened by a Port Health team at anchorage.
- In case of recently arrived crew on board the ship (within the last 16 days), the Harbour Master will decide, based upon the submitted facts, whether pilot boarding and port entry are allowed.
- No disembarkation of ship’s crew is allowed during the ship’s call, including the anchorage.
- In case of needed emergency shore leave or crew change, pre-approval is needed from the Harbour Master, Immigration and Port Health. For Harbour Master approval, this request must be sent to the Port Control email address as mentioned hereunder. Approval is given by email.
- Any concerned staff interacting with the ship’s crew should follow up on the official advice from the Ministry of Health and the World Health Organization on personal protection.
- Port Control should be contacted in case of any suspicious situation regarding the Coronavirus in the port area or onboard a ship so that appropriate measures can be taken in close cooperation with the Port Health team.

Headline: Hurricane Isaias to Impact Florida Coast this Weekend Before Moving up the Eastern Seaboard
Details:
Hurricane Isaias is continuing to strengthen as it moves through the Bahamas towards the east Florida coast. The storm is currently a Category 1 hurricane on the Saffir-Simpson wind scale, with winds of at least 75 miles per hour. Strengthening is expected beginning Friday night and the storm may increase to a Category 2 hurricane. The current forecast shows Isaias skirting the east coast of Florida beginning Saturday night before moving up the East Coast. Landfall is currently forecast sometime on Monday near the South Carolina-North Carolina border. Isaias will then weaken into a tropical storm and is expected to continue moving up the coast, potentially impacting the Northeast coast. Some uncertainty in the track of the storm remains and its possible the storm makes landfall along the upper east coast of Florida late Sunday in addition to the expected landfall in the Carolinas. The National Hurricane Center (NHC) has issued a hurricane warning for portions of the central and southern Atlantic Florida coasts. A state of emergency has been issued for the entire eastern Florida coast as well as for the states of North Carolina and Virginia. 



Assessment: As of this writing, the only evacuations issued are on Ocracoke Island in North Carolina. Evacuations remain a possibility for the coast of Florida as the storm continues to move closer to land and the hurricane track evolves. Airport closures and flight delays also remain a possibility both along the eastern coast of Florida, as well as up the rest of the East Coast as the storm moves up the coastline. Portions of Florida and the Carolinas are forecast to see upwards of five inches of rain and flash flooding is possible along the entire east coast of the United States. Similarly, port closures remain a possibility but as of this writing, none have been issued. Several ports in Florida, South Carolina, North Carolina, and Virginia have been set to Port Condition Whiskey. This means that ports remain open to all commercial and cargo operations but commercial vessels greater than 500 gross tons should begin making plans to depart the port. The strong winds from Isaias are likely to cause widespread power outages across the eastern seaboard. Some outages may be prolonged for multiple days depending on other impacts caused by the storm. Those with interests along the U.S. East Coast are advised to continue monitoring the situation closely. The public should use extreme caution in storm conditions and heed all weather warnings and instructions from local authorities.

Headline: UPDATE 10 - Vietnam – Recovery efforts are underway after Tropical Storm Sinlaku caused flooding. Event closed.
Details:
Sources indicate that recovery efforts are underway across Vietnam after the passage of Tropical Storm Sinlaku caused flooding and landslides in multiple provinces. Over 2,800 structures were damaged, destroyed, or inundated to some capacity, while seven people were killed, and eight people were injured in storm-related incidents. The major impacts by province were as follows:

- An Giang: At least 19 homes were destroyed and two people were injured.

- Bac Lieu: Up to 87 homes were damaged.

- Ca Mau: At least 49 homes were destroyed, while 375 homes were damaged. The districts most heavily impacted were Dam Doi and Tran Van Thoi.

- Can Tho: At least 12 homes were destroyed, while 88 others were damaged in Can Tho City.

- Dak Lak: Approximately 930 homes were inundated.

- Hai Phong: Flooding was reported in Hai Phong City resulting in an unspecified number of local evacuations.

- Hoa Binh: One person was killed after being swept away by floodwaters in Tu Son commune in Kim Boi District.

- Kien Giang: At least three people died, and four others were injured. Up to 653 homes were impacted by flooding, with 175 destroyed, 446 damaged, and 32 inundated. At least 116 households were evacuated due to landslide risks in Kien Luong District.

- Lam Dong: One person was injured in Da Lat due to falling trees striking homes.

- Lao Cai: Two people were killed, and one home was damaged in a landslide in Bat Xat District.

- Nghe An: Up to 16,200 people were evacuated from low-lying areas in the province. Approximately 16 bridges were damaged by floodwaters in Quy Chau District. 

- Quang Ninh: One person was killed in Ha Long. An unspecified number of people were evacuated from low-lying areas near waterways.

- Soc Trang: Flooding and landslides damaged at least 271 buildings, particularly in the districts of My Xuyen, My Tu, Soc Trang City, and Nga Nam. One person was injured.

- Tra Vinh: Flooding and landslides damaged approximately 300 homes across the province, with 23 of them destroyed.

- Yen Bai: At least 20 homes were damaged by landslides across the province. This event is closed.

Headline: Port workers in Valparaiso threaten to resume 35-day strike
Details:
On November 17, 2018 more than 500 casual workers at Chile's flagship port of Valparaiso decided to walk off the job to demand a bonus payment, more formal contracts, and improved working conditions. After a series of small demonstrations, around 50 dockworkers linked to Terminal Cerros de Valparaiso (TCVAL) finally accepted an offer put forward by the port operator and returned to work on November 30. The rest of the protesting workers, however, did not reach an agreement with Terminal Pacífico Sur (TPS), the second and most important concessionaire in Valparaiso, until December 21, 2018, which shut down shipping for over 35 days at one of Chile’s most important ports and a major commercial hub to the capital city Santiago.

The first weeks of the strike were marked by small pickets outside the port facilities and union leaders negotiating with TPS representatives. In recent weeks, however, protests in Valparaiso have turned increasingly violent and spread to other ports along the nation's Pacific coast. The conflict reached a tipping point on Monday, December 19, when strikers set barricades throughout the city and police agents repressed demonstrators with water cannons and tear gas. Protesters also got into the Dockers' Union headquarters, resulting in 20 detainees, two injured, and the destruction of much of the furniture in the building.

One day after the violent protests in Valparaiso, the striking dockworkers received support from their colleagues at the northern ports of Iquique, Antofagasta, Caldera, Ventanas, and San Antonio, the most important one in the country and close to Valparaiso.  In the southern part of the country, dockworkers at the ports of Talcahuano San Vicente and Puerto Montt also stopped their work in support of their colleagues in Valparaiso. The possibility of officially extending the strike to other ports in the country triggered alarms in sectors highly dependent on export activity, such as agriculture, food processing, and chemicals, which send products worth some USD 25 billion to foreign markets each year.

Impacts

According to the Chilean Maritime Port Organization, the strike has caused more than 50,000 containers to be diverted to other ports, with a total revenue loss of over USD 8 million. Chile’s fruit sector was particularly impacted by the strike in Valparaiso, which handles approximately 55% of Chile’s fruit exports. According to the Federation of Fruit Producers of Chile, fruit shipments from the port of Valparaiso fell 95% as a result of the port strike, going from 59,883 tons between November 16 and December 17 in 2017 to only 3,006 tons in 2018.

Meanwhile, there was a large increase in shipments at the port of San Antonio, which had already displaced Valparaiso in cargo handling and efficiency due to past port conflicts. However, not all was positive news for the Port of San Antonio, which suffered from increased congestion due to more than 20,000 additional trucks that arrived during the strike. In a normal day, according to San Antonio’s Port Authority, there are about 100 to 150 trucks that are served in an hour. However, due to the massive arrival of operators from Valparaiso, it was necessary to attend to more than 300 trucks in just one hour.

Outlook

On December 19, the dockworkers union and the port operator TPS reached a pre-agreement, which was later rejected by the dockworkers at a general assembly. The workers argued that the compensations offered by TPS are far below what they demand. Nonetheless, on December 22, workers at port of Valparaiso ended their strike, when union representatives accepted an offer from the operator, TPS, following an agreement signed between the workers and the Ministry of Labor. TPS’s offer includes a bonus of around 760,000 pesos (USD 1,100 or EUR 965), a gift card of 250,000 pesos (USD 365 or EUR 320) and a training course worth over 400,000 pesos (USD 600 or EUR 525).

On January 3, however, a group of port workers resumed demonstrations in Valparaiso, placing barricades near the Dockworkers' Union headquarters. Protesters reportedly claim that port officials have not adhered to an initial payment agreement reached two weeks ago and that as many as 22 dockworkers who participated in the December demonstrations have been denied access to the port facilities. On the same day, TPS issued a public statement confirming that the Port of Valparaiso has continued to operate normally despite the most recent demonstrations.

Lasting 35 days, the 2018 November-December strike at the Port of Valparaiso was the second longest port strike in Chile in the last 20 years and one with important implications for the fruit industry in the country. Supply chain managers should continue to monitor the situation at the Port of Valparaiso because although operations have resumed, further demonstrations are expected in the upcoming days. Moreover, it will take weeks, if not months, to clear the congestion created as a result of the service disruption in Valparaiso.

Headline: Floods to disrupt rail freight traffic Algeciras-Madrid until January
Details: Local authorities in Spain confirmed that rail freight services between the Port of Algaeciras, the largest in Spain, and the city of Madrid are suffering serious disruptions until January 2019 due to flood damages to the rail track between Port of Algeciras and Antequera. The most affected area of the rail track is the kilometer point 3/100, where the river Tinajas flooded, sweeping away the ground under the rail track. Government officials announced that they are currently looking into an alternative route via Seville while it completes the restoration of the damaged rail track. Those customers shipping through the Port of Algaeciras should anticipate visible delays and should plan accordingly.

Headline: ReCAAP Report: Coronavirus Pandemic Causes Piracy Incidents to Double; Trend Likely to Continue
Details:
On Thursday, the Regional Cooperation Agreement on Combating Piracy and Armed Robbery against Ships in Asia (ReCAAP) released a report indicating the number of piracy incidents in Asian waters nearly doubled in the first six months of 2020 compared to the same period last year. According to the ReCAAP report, there were 51 incidents between January and June—compared to 28 in 2019—with 16 reported in the Singapore Strait alone. Of the 51 piracy incidents, 49 were incidents of armed robbery against ships, while two were piracy incidents; ReCAAP defines incidents as piracy if they occur outside the jurisdiction of any state, while those occurring in territorial waters are considered armed robbery. In addition to the Singapore Strait, incidents also occurred off the coast of Bangladesh, India, Indonesia, the Philippines, and Vietnam, as well as in the South China Sea. The report attributed the increase to the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic and its impact on global trade.



Assessment: With the COVID-19 pandemic currently showing no signs of slowing, the associated financial hardship facing individuals impacted by the economic downturn is unlikely to ease in the near term. When coupled with the fact that commercial vessels are expected to be less secured as maritime shipping companies look to cut costs, growing poverty and unemployment could perpetuate the uptick in piracy in Asian waters in the near and medium-term future. Compared to the Horn of Africa, piracy incidents in Asia appear to be more opportunistic, often perpetrated by local fishermen merely looking to supplement their incomes by stealing scrap metal, engine parts, and communication equipment from ships and selling the pilfered items on the black market. Additionally, most piracy remains non-violent, though perpetrators have sometimes abducted crew members and held them for ransom. Therefore, mariners operating in the region should exercise a high level of vigilance at all times and ensure that appropriate security measures are in place to deter potential attackers.

Headline: Port of Rotterdam moderately tightens admission rules for vessels
Details:
Sources indicated on April 9 that as a precautionary measure against the spread of the COVID-19 coronavirus pandemic, the Port of Rotterdam issued moderately tightened restrictions on vessel admission for an unknown duration. The measures are as follows: 

Cargo vessels must issue a Maritime Declaration of Health (MDOH) to the Harbour Coordination Center (HCC). If a crew member is declared to be exhibiting mild symptoms, the crew member will be isolated from the rest of the crew. If the crewmember cannot be isolated, the crewmember may be transferred to shore and potentially admitted to a hospital if needed. Shore leave is permitted for crewmembers only for medical reasons, and only medical professionals, maintenance staff, and government employees may board the vessel. Crew changes are still permitted, but must be executed as far as possible via the landward side. Cargo operations can continue, even when a crewmember has tested positive for COVID-19. However, in such cases, no crewmember may come in contact with port personnel. Vessel departure permission for crew with positive COVID-19 cases will be determined on a case-by-case basis.

Headline: UPDATE: Truck drivers at Port of Los Angeles began 3-day strike on October 1
Details: Updated sources continue to report that Los Angeles and Long Beach port truck drivers and warehouse workers commenced a 3-day strike at 07:00 local time on Monday, October 1. Picketing has been reported at XPO and NFI facilities, marine terminals, rail yards, customer warehouses and distribution centers. The strike was called for to protest against the misclassification of workers as independent contractors, instead of as employees, by the trucking companies they work for. Truckers classified as contractors are not eligible for a minimum wage, or forego benefits such as health insurance or holiday pay. This is the 16 th strike staged by Justice for Port Drivers in the past five years. The previous strikes resulted in minimal or no impact on cargo flow at the port complex. Port police have reportedly been positioned at terminals to ensure operations can continue during these strikes. As of late Monday morning, a spokesperson for the Port of Los Angeles stated that there has been no impact on cargo flow. Headline: Flood-Related Disruptions, Warnings to Linger Despite Improving Weather, Death Toll at Seven
Details:
Flood warnings remained in effect across North Carolina on Friday after a weather system tied to Tropical Storm Eta brought more than nine inches of rainfall to parts of the state on November 11-12. The National Weather Service extended a flash flood warning for the central counties of Alamance, Chatham, Durham, Johnston, Orange, and Wake until 3:45 PM local time on November 13, while local authorities have advised that several rivers, including the Cape Fear, Haw, Neuse, and Tar, will crest between flood stage and major flood stage over the weekend. In addition to rising water levels, multiple stretches of highway and surface streets remain closed or impassable due to flooding. Affected highways of note include Interstate 95, with the northbound lanes closed near mile marker 102 in Johnston County, about 30 miles southeast of Raleigh, until at least 5:00 PM local time on Friday. Another part of I-95 was closed near Wilson but has since reopened, as have parts of Interstate 85 near Charlotte. To view up-to-date road conditions, one can consult the following webpage maintained by the North Carolina Department of Transportation: https://www.drivenc.gov/#incidents.



Five counties declared states of emergency on Thursday due to the deluge: Alexander, Burke, Catawba, Iredell, and Yadkin. Among the areas hardest hit was Alexander County, about 65 miles northwest of Charlotte, where three people died and 31 others were rescued when floodwaters from a nearby river inundated a campsite and swept away recreational vehicles and those inside. Elsewhere in Alexander County, another person died in a car accident that was attributed to a bridge washout, while a child reportedly drowned in a swollen creek in Wake County near Raleigh. At the time of this writing, the death toll from the rainfall-induced flooding stood at seven, with two others missing. Additionally, hundreds of other people were evacuated or rescued statewide, including 143 students from the Charlotte Corvian Community School, while more than 16,400 homes and businesses lost electricity. Dozens of schools delayed the start of classes or shifted to virtual learning only on Thursday due to the inclement weather, while others in the eastern part of the state closed early once the rainfall began. The weather system, a combination of tropical moisture from Eta and a cold front, also affected parts of South Carolina and Virginia. In the former, several people had to be rescued from flooded homes in York County, while southeastern Virginia saw intense rainfall and flooding as well; flood warnings were still in place on Friday.



Assessment: Conditions improved across the southeastern U.S. on Friday and drier weather is forecast throughout the region into next week, presumably facilitating recovery and clean-up efforts. Indeed, power appeared to have been restored to the vast majority of affected customers by Friday morning; however, as noted above, the threat of flooding and associated disruptions will persist in the coming days. With swollen rivers projected to crest on Saturday, water levels are unlikely to recede before Sunday, especially from low-lying roads and neighborhoods. As such, with further residential flooding and road closures almost certain over the weekend, the public should allow additional time for overland travel and exercise caution when driving, taking care not to drive around barricades or on flooded roads, particularly those covered by moving water.

Headline: Booms Placed After Oil from Decommissioned Pipeline Leaked into Sea at Port Dickson
Details:
Officials on Wednesday confirmed that a black substance discovered in monsoon storm drains in the Kampung Gelam area of Port Dickson, south of Kuala Lumpur, on Sunday was crude oil. The oil leaked from decommissioned pipelines connected to a refinery in the area after the pipes were punctured during construction work. Repair work to the pipes was expected to be completed on Wednesday.



Assessment: Some of the oil from the leak flowed into the nearby sea. Authorities have placed booms in the area to stop additional flow into the ocean. Following the repairs to the broken section of pipeline, work will be carried out to flush remaining crude oil from the pipes. Sand will be used to replace contaminated earth near the leak. Officials have not yet reported how much oil actually leaked or made it into the ocean. While there has been no immediate indication that this was a major spill, disruptions are possible in the area while cleanup operations are ongoing.

Headline: Ongoing Tensions Sustain the Risk of Clashes at Weekend Protests in Europe over Racial Justice
Details:
Protest activity in recent weeks related to the Black Lives Matter movement and associated local grievances in several European countries is planned to continue through the coming weekend. Hotspots of recent protest activity with flare-ups around demonstrations, such as in London and Paris, are likely to remain so. Police in Paris have prohibited three demonstrations planned for Saturday, though gatherings are likely to occur regardless of the prohibition, raising the potential for confrontations and clashes with authorities. Potentially adding to tensions, the French government walked back plans to prohibit chokeholds by police until a replacement method is found. Additional clashes between opposing groups in London may occur, while police may take swift action to quell unruly behavior. London authorities have arrested nearly 230 people in connection to protests in recent weeks. Some prominent German politicians have rejected alleged systemic racism among police forces, and disputes over calls for reform can further demonstration activity in the near term. As well as central squares, government buildings, and US diplomatic facilities in several European countries, protests and associated escalations have frequently occurred around controversial statues and other symbols. Sites connected with colonial history have been common targets of condemnation. 



Assessment: The bulk of demonstrators have been peaceful, though clashes with counter-protesters and police remain a risk. Authorities continue to be challenged by allowing peaceful protest while trying to deter actions that could result in unrest, as well as the ongoing difficulty of large crowds developing while COVID-19 restrictions on gatherings remain in effect. Scrutiny over policing methods and accusations of systemic racism are likely to prompt additional demonstrations by officers, and discontent among officers could results in actions such as increased sick calls, as has occurred in limited instances in the United States. Recent protests over alleged police violence and racial inequalities have also drawn attention to the lack of official data held by countries such as France and Germany, due to policies against the collection of ethnicity in demographic data, that could underscore disparities. With mobilizations continuing over the coming days, it is advised to avoid protest activity as a precaution and to anticipate potential disruption in proximity to demonstrations.

Headline: Singapore port authorities revise detailed guidelines for crew changes amid COVID-19 outbreak
Details:
Media sources report that the port authorities of Singapore will be implementing detailed guidelines for crew changes due to the recent cases of crew members who are tested positive for COVID-19 upon arrival in Singapore. The new measures will include the need for the signing-on crew to self-isolate for the 14 days before departing for Singapore, ship-owners, managers, and agents ensuring accurate COVID-19 Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) tests, and direct transfers to the ship upon arrival in Singapore.
With immediate effect, the authorities will give priority to applications from Singapore registered ships and applications for sign-off crew only (i.e. without signing-on new crew). For all other cases, the authorities will consider the following circumstances for crew change applications:

(a) the crew has served his/her maximum time on board and no further extension of the employment contract is granted by the flag State; or
(b) compassionate grounds e.g. death of an immediate family member; or
(c) the crew is no longer medically fit to work onboard the ship.

Cargo ships meeting the above criteria and circumstances may submit their applications to MPA by filling up the online form at least 14 days before the planned crew changes, at www.mpa.gov.sg/web/portal/home/port-ofsingapore/operations/crew-change.

Headline: UPDATE 10 - Jakarta & West Java – Flooding has subsided in Sukabumi and Central Jakarta; no major rain expected.
Details:
Updated Report:

Media sources are reporting that the flooding in Sukabumi and Central Jakarta has subsided and that the Emergency Response status was revoked on Monday. No major rains are expected throughout today. Aid is still being distributed to those impacted in the area.

Previous Updates:

Sources reported that heavy rainfall caused flooding in multiple locations across Jakarta Province and West Java Province. The Meteorology, Climatology and Geophysics Agency (BMKG) expects heavy rain to fall throughout Jakarta and West Java Province through Wednesday, September 30. As a result, local government agencies continue to expect associated disruptions and damages to take place in the most affected areas. Flood relief efforts continue throughout the region, with local government delivering food parcels and structural assistants.

Sources reported that all missing persons in Sukabumi District in West Java Province have been found, but three were killed. Twenty other people in Sukabumi were injured. Emergency services have called off search and rescue missions in the area. At least 34 shelters have been set up in Central Jakarta for residents within the most severely impacted areas. Impacted areas include Tanah Abang, Benhil, Petamburan, and Karet Tengsin, as well as residential areas near the Ciliwung River such as Kartini and Pasar Baru In addition, the Central Jakarta City Government has ordered the dredging of waterways, as well as the repair of several supporting infrastructures. 

At least 210 families have been displaced in Sukabumi. The Pabrik PT. Aqua Golden Mississippi factory in Bogor, West Java has been reopened after flash flooding caused the facility to close for several days. The Ciliwung River has reportedly overflown near Kebon Pala, causing inundation in several areas. In addition, the Cianten River also overflowed which caused severe inundation in the Cibunian Village, Pamijahan District.

Headline: Counter-fuel theft campaign leaves 60+ tankers stranded at Mexican ports
Details: Local media sources indicate on January 11 that the counter-fuel theft campaign launched across Mexico has left over 60 tankers stranded outside the country's ports due to inability to unload. The counter-fuel theft campaign involves the use of trucks as opposed to the previously favored pipelines, which were more theft-prone, yet allowed storage facilities to be quickly replenished at ports. The problem is anticipated to worsen, with more vessels arriving carrying 350,000-400,000 barrels and requiring USD 30,000-50,000 per day for operation. Those involved in the petroleum trade in Mexico should anticipate worsening delays at the ports and should plan accordingly.

Headline: US Consulate General in Chennai Issued a Weather Alert About Forecast Tropical Cyclone
Details:
On Monday, the US Consulate General in Chennai issued the following Weather Alert:



“Location:   Puducherry, Tamil Nadu



Event:   A tropical depression in the Bay of Bengal is expected to strengthen into a tropical cyclone (Tropical Cyclone Nivar), making landfall in Tamil Nadu by November 25, 2020. According to local weather sources, such as the Regional Specialized Meteorological Centre for Tropical Cyclones Over North Indian Ocean (http://www.rsmcnewdelhi.imd.gov.in/index.php?lang=en), heavy rains may begin as early as November 24, 2020.  The cyclone is expected to move north and west, along the coast.  There is an increased risk of heavy rainfall, flooding and high winds for both coastal and inland locations.  Internet service, landline phone and cell phone capabilities may be affected.



U.S. Consulate General Chennai staff members have been asked to defer non-essential travel and to make preparations should sheltering-in-place or relocation become necessary.



Consulate Operations:  The U.S. Consulate General Chennai will be closed to the public for visa, U.S. citizen and foreign commercial services on Wednesday, November 25, 2020, due to the effects of likely heavy wind and rain, and is closed on Thursday, November 26, 2020, due to the Thanksgiving holiday.  The Consulate is currently scheduled to re-open to the public on Friday, November 27, 2020.



Actions to Take:



Monitor local media for weather updates.

Seek secure shelter.

Have evacuation plans that do not rely on U.S. government assistance.

Notify friends and family of your safety.”



The full text of the alert can be viewed here: https://in.usembassy.gov/weather-alert-tropical-cyclone-development-november-23-2020/

Headline: El Salvador – Flooding has been reported in Medica municipality. - UPDATE 3
Details:

Updated social media reports indicated heavy flooding in the Medica municipality of San Salvador. Expect possible residual disruptions. This event is closed.

Significant flooding was reported along Av Morazan in Sonsonate municipality following heavy rainfall in the area. No injuries or widespread evacuations were immediately indicated.  

Previous flooding caused by heavy rains from Tropical Storm Amanda killed up to 30 people in El Salvador. Reports indicated that structural damage and fallen trees were reported in the Aguilares area, and that the Acelhuate River was swollen. Three homes were reportedly destroyed in the area. In the Bolivar canton, trees fell on several homes. Streets leading to the Bolivar and Las Tunas cantons were blocked due to fallen trees. At least 60 shelters were open as recovery operations continue. Approximately 11,179 people were evacuated, with most evacuees having been reported in San Salvador, while the other evacuees were from the departments of La Libertad, Sonsonate, and San Vicente. Evacuations were also reported in San Jeronimo, in the Metapan area. At least 2,603 houses were damaged, including 582 damaged or destroyed in Campos Verdes II in Lourdes, Colon. Six bridges were also damaged, with most of them located in La Libertad.

Headline: Three Attempted Acts of Piracy in Singapore Strait Overnight Sunday into Monday Amid Slight Uptick
Details:
Beginning at around 11:00 PM local time on Sunday, there were three attempted acts of piracy in the Singapore Strait in a roughly two-and-a-half-hour period. Each of the situations took place off the Indonesian coast and all three involved ships in the eastbound lane of the Strait’s Traffic Separation Scheme (TSS). The first and third occurred near Nongsa Point, and the second happened off of Pulau Nongsa. Nothing was successfully stolen during any of the attempts, and there were no injuries.



Assessment: According to the Regional Cooperation Agreement on Combating Piracy and Armed Robbery Against Ships in Asia (ReCAAP), there has been a slight uptick in recent reports of piracy in the Singapore Strait, with October’s six total incidents being the highest monthly number for the year thus far. No injuries have been reported in any of the October incidents, and suspects successfully stole minor items in only one of the attacks. There have been a total of 28 piracy attempts reported in the Strait so far in 2020, compared to 31 for the entirety of 2019. Of this year’s attacks, 24 have taken place against ships traveling in the eastbound lanes of the TSS. Given the short timeframe that the Sunday night attempts occurred in, they were likely carried out by a single group of suspects. Although there were no injuries, the crew of one of the ships was unsure of whether all of the suspects had departed, and the ship was forced to divert to Batam, Indonesia, where it was searched by Indonesian naval personnel. Such diversions could cause significant disruptions for shipping even when there are no injuries and nothing is successfully stolen. As no arrests were made in any of Sunday night’s attempts, ReCAAP has warned that the same suspects may possibly try to attack additional ships. The organization advises ships in the region to take precautions and to report any incidents of piracy to the nearest government.

Headline: UPDATE 4: Thousands continue to protest against Duque and Cali curfew amid nationwide strike
Details: Updated media sources that thousands of protesters marched in Colombia’s main cities in protest against President Ivan Duque following a day that ended in roadblocks and vandalism that forced the decree of a curfew int he city of Cali. The protest has not affected key sectors of the economy such as oil and coal production, although transport routes have been reduced considerably according to the government. Previous media sources indicated on November 21 that the nationwide general strike began in Colombia. The demonstration was initially organized by university students but has grown to several groups to denounce the economic and social policies of President Ivan Duque. Massive demonstrations were reported in Bogota, Barranquilla, Cartagena, Medellin, and Cali where people are marching towards city centers. In Bogota, marches started in the financial district in the direction of the Plaza de Bolivar. Police clashed with protesters as they blocked Suba Avenue. In Barranquilla, protesters divided into three marches starting in Esthercita Forero Park, Autonomous University, and the Rincon Latino neighborhood all heading towards Paseo Bolivar (the city center). In Cartagena, protesters marched on the Pedro de Heredia Avenue and congregating in the historic city center. Workers and students are protesting against a slew of economic reforms that the president has implemented including eliminating the state pension fund, increasing the retirement age, and hiring young people with salaries below the minimum wage. Social organizations are demanding a greater commitment from the government to implement the peace agreement with the FARC.

Do not take undue risks and anticipate disruption to travel for several days.

According to the National Hurricane Centre (NHC), the storm is nearing Category 5 status with sustained winds of around 140mph recorded. Officials are warning residents in the path of the storm 'not to underestimate the threat'. Even if the storm does not reach the Category 5 threshold (winds in excess of 157mph), the NHC states 'there remains high confidence that Florence will be a large and extremely dangerous hurricane'. The National Guard has been activated in the states affected and residents have started boarding homes. While there are also reports of long queues at fuel stations and supermarkets/hardware stores being depleted of stock. South Carolina Governor, Henry McMaster, has confirmed that government offices, including schools and medical facilities will be closed. Travellers are advised to 'Know Your Evacuation Zone' by monitoring local emergency management websites and associated media reports. Do not take undue risks and anticipate disruption to travel for several days.

Headline: Several Countries Begin Lifting COVID-19 Restrictions, Despite Rising Cases and Warnings
Details:
On Monday, several countries in Sub-Saharan Africa began lifting their lockdowns and other restrictions introduced to contain the spread of COVID-19. Ghana lifted its three-week restriction on movement in the Accra and Kumasi metropolitan areas on Monday, while Madagascar began progressively lifting the confinements in Antananarivo, Fianarantsoa, and Toamasina. In Madagascar, public transportation was expected to resume on Monday and schools will reopen on Wednesday. The restrictions on movement will also be lifted from 6:00 AM to 1:00 PM local time daily; however, the ban on inter-city travel will remain in place and everyone must wear face masks in public. Additionally, Burkina Faso began reopening public markets, which had been closed since March 25. While Zimbabwe and South Africa have extended their lockdowns, both have eased the restrictions slightly. Zimbabwe extended its lockdown until May 3 but will allow mining operations to fully resume. The lockdown in South Africa also remains in effect until April 30, but authorities have stated that port operations will resume to decrease congestion. South Africa also began allowing mining companies to resume partial operations last week.



Assessment: Countries across Sub-Saharan Africa have faced increasing pressure to lift the restrictions from within the local populace, many of whom perceive the measures as affected their livelihoods. While the lifting of the measures is likely to help ease tensions somewhat, health officials have warned that lifting them too soon could lead to a rise in new cases. Much of Sub-Saharan Africa continues to experience exponential increases in cases and testing capabilities remain extremely limited, making the region particularly vulnerable to widespread, under-reported community transmission. Ghana may be one of the few exceptions, as it has ramped up testing significantly, testing over 60,000 people, and has adopted aggressive contact tracing. South Africa has also stepped up testing in recent weeks, and coupled with its lockdown, it appears to have helped stem the number of new cases per day.

Headline: UPDATE 1 - Grenade explosions in Antwerp likely indicative of drug gang rivalry, increasing security risks in Belgian port areas
Details: On 24 August 2020, unidentified perpetrators threw a hand grenade into a vacant building in Deurne, east Antwerp, with the grenade bouncing back and exploding on the street next to the house of a local drug trafficking gang leader, without causing any casualties. The attack followed two other hand grenade explosions over the weekend in east Antwerp’s Ekstelaar and Borgerhout areas, where a shooting targeting the family home of a drug gang member also took place, not leading to any casualties. Prior to the incidents, the police had seized a shipment of 500kg of cocaine at the port and detained two port employees suspected of having facilitated the trafficking of up to 800kg of cocaine, as part of a separate investigation. In 2019, Belgian authorities had seized a record 62 tonnes of cocaine in total, a 23% increase compared to 2018. The Port of Antwerp is the principal entry point for cocaine in Europe, with the substance mostly being trafficked from Brazil, Colombia and Ecuador.Significance: The increase in frequency of violent attacks between criminal gangs with the deployment of hand grenades in residential areas of Antwerp is likely indicative of intensifying rivalry between groups controlling the trafficking of cocaine into Europe through the Port of Antwerp. The escalation is likely to be linked to changes in the dynamics of drug trafficking gangs, particularly of influential drug cartels in Latin America; their revenues from extortion reduced during lockdowns introduced globally from March in response to the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) outbreak. While violent attacks between gangs have so far been mostly limited to residential areas in east Antwerp, the escalation increases the likelihood of violent confrontations, including shootings and hand grenade deployment, spreading to port facilities where cargo is handled and the trafficking takes place. An increase in the frequency of checks conducted on containers by Antwerp port authorities as a response to the hand grenade attacks would probably mitigate the risk, resulting in more significant drug seizures and detention of suspected traffickers, acting as a deterrent and disrupting the illegal drug route through the port, although probably only temporarily. However, this would also lead to longer security procedures at the port, likely slowing down the handling of cargo containers. Headline: Cleanup Underway Following Strong Storm That Killed Three in Melbourne Metro Area
Details:
A strong windstorm that passed through the Melbourne metro area late on Thursday led to three deaths and at least one injury. The deaths were reported in the Blackburn South, Fernshaw, and Tecoma suburbs, while other heavily affected areas included Belgrave, Croydon, Lilydale, Mount Evelyn, and Mount Waverley. Dozens of buildings and vehicles were damaged, and power was temporarily disrupted for up to 80,000 customers. The power outages also led to undisinfected water entering the water system, and around 250,000 Yarra Valley Water customers in up to 88 northern and eastern suburbs were placed under a boil water advisory, which remained in place for at least some areas as of Saturday morning. Power was later restored.



Assessment: Most of the damage was caused by high winds. Gusts of up to 100 miles per hour were reported. All three of the deaths were caused by falling trees, with at least one person killed while driving when a tree struck their vehicle. Due to the boil water advisory, shortages of bottled water were reported in multiple stores in the area as customers bought large amounts. While the advisory remains in effect, authorities urge residents to boil any water used for drinking or cooking. Emergency drinking water is also available from Yarra Valley Water if necessary. No additional strong storms are currently forecast for the Melbourne area over the next several days. Individuals are advised to follow the directions of authorities in any emergency situation and to expect possible residual traffic disruptions in areas with fallen trees.

Headline: Cambodia – Recovery efforts are underway after flooding killed up to 44 people. - UPDATE 6
Details:
Sources indicate that recovery efforts continue across Cambodia after flooding killed up to 44 people. Flooding has largely subsided and normal operations are resuming. Expect possible residual disruptions. This event is closed.  


At least 26 of the deaths occurred in Banteay Meanchey, seven were reported in Kampong Thom, and six in Pursat. Deaths were also recorded in Sihanoukville, Pailin, Kampong Chhnang, and Stung Treng. Approximately 133,203 homes were damaged or destroyed. In addition, more than 594,388 people have been affected by the flooding, of whom 47,580 were evacuated or displaced, including over 500 from Phnom Penh. Approximately 912,333 acres of crops have been inundated, while at least 951 schools were affected.

Flooding began around Thursday, October 1, following the passage of Tropical Storm Noul, and has affected at least 20 provinces. The provinces impacted include Phnom Penh, Pursat, Pailin, Banteay Meanchey, Battambang, Svay Rieng, Thbong Khmum, Oddar Meanchey, Siem Reap, Takeo, Kampong Speu, Mondulkiri, Sihanoukville, Koh Kong, Preah Vihear, Stung Treng, Kampong Cham, Kandal, Kampong Chhnang, and Kampong Thom. The flooding has also inundated and damaged numerous roads. At least 40 unspecified factories reportedly closed across Kampong Speu Province, Kandal Province, and Phnom Penh.

Headline: Hapag-Lloyd suspends overseas agricultural container shipments from North America
Details: Shipping sources on October 26 report that the German international shipping and transportation company Hapag-Lloyd indicated to exporters that it will be suspending overseas agricultural container shipments from North America. Hapag-Lloyd has decided it needs to quickly reposition empty containers back to Asian shipping centers, even if it means forgoing hauling critical food and agriculture products back to manufacturers overseas. This will likely impact exporters in the Minneapolis-St. Paul region. The majority of Hapag-Lloyd delivered agricultural shipments go to food processing customers in Japan, Indonesia, Hong Kong, Taiwan and Malaysia.

Headline: Protected industrial action at DP World Fremantle
Details:

The work restrictions include various bans on employees working in tasks above their normal grade, overtime, shift extensions, accepting late call-ins and ceasing advanced or delayed start times. The latest update of the PIA includes:

- Ban on the performance of work on all vessels from 6am on 25 December until 2pm on 27 December

- Ban on the performance of work on all vessels from 10pm on 27 December until 10pm on 28 December

- Ban on the performance of work on all vessels on day shift from 6am from 29 December for indefinite period

- Ban on the performance of work on all vessels from 2pm on 1 January until 2pm on 2 January

- All terminal operations will be stopped during these hours.

- Work restrictions apply.

Headline: UPDATE 1 - LNG tanker attack indicates increasing piracy and kidnap risks affecting onshore assets in Equatorial Guinea
Details: The Equatoguinean government on 17 October announced that armed pirates attacked the Marshall Islands-flagged LNG tanker Methane Princess in anchorage. The pirates reportedly boarded the vessel at the Punta Europa LNG Terminal off Malabo on Bioko Island, Equatorial Guinea’s main LNG marine pier, while it was completing a cargo operation. Reports indicate that the attackers took hostages, including an Equatoguinean and a Filipino, while another Equatoguinean citizen suffered minor injuries. The latest incident follows a growing trend of piracy and kidnap-for-ransom by criminal gangs in Equatoguinean maritime waters and the wider Gulf of Guinea, with similar piracy incidents reported close to Lomé in Togo and Takoradi in Ghana. In May, gunmen boarded the Comoros-flagged general cargo vessel Rio Mitong at anchor near Malabo and foreign and local crew members were abducted. In addition, the Equatorial Guinea-flagged ro-ro vessel Djibloho was attacked off the coast of Luba, Bioko Island, in the same month. Likewise, pirates attacked oil-supply vessel Pacific Warden near Luba in November 2019 and abducted seven out of 15 crew members. In May 2019, pirates boarded heavy-load carrier ship Blue Marlin, but later fled following a gunfight with the Spanish and Equatoguinean navies, with 10 pirates being arrested. Significance: The latest attack at the LNG terminal indicates growing operational reach and capability of these mostly Niger Delta-based assailants, while exposing security shortcomings at a strategic national asset. IHS Markit assesses that such attacks are likely to increase in frequency and would involve crew abductions and robbery of valuables other than fuel cargo. Such attacks are likely to be driven by increased investments in major energy infrastructure projects, such as the proposed development of a Gas Mega Hub.
